course.title: TypeScript and Node.js
course.description: How TypeScript's types catch mistakes before code runs, and how Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, ending with a small typed service that validates what enters it.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read JavaScript (the language lessons of the-web-html-css-javascript, or equivalent) and has used a command line.

paragraphs: TypeScript adds labels to JavaScript, and a compiler reads those labels before the program runs. Every label is removed again when the JavaScript is written, so the types catch mistakes while you type and cost nothing at run time. This course shows what the compiler infers, how it narrows a value that could be one of several types, and how types can be derived from one another so that each fact is written once.

Node.js is the second half of the subject. It runs JavaScript outside a browser, on one thread, with a fixed order for the callbacks that wait their turn, and with streams that move data in chunks so that a large file never has to sit in memory. The middle lessons follow that thread from modules and environment variables through the event loop, bytes, HTTP handlers, promises and packages, and each rule is short enough to apply by hand.

The last lesson combines the two into a small service that checks its configuration and every request at the boundary and stops without dropping work. TypeScript and JavaScript cannot run inside the lessons, so every question about code asks you to read it and say what it prints, what type the compiler reports or which line is at fault. The answers were checked with the compiler and with Node, and the lessons explain the rule behind each one.
outcomes: You'll be able to predict the type TypeScript infers and read its error messages.
You'll be able to narrow unions, write generics and derive types from other types.
You'll be able to predict the order of callbacks in Node and what blocks the event loop.
You'll be able to read an HTTP handler, a stream and a semver range, and design a service that validates its input.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on The Web: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. You should be able to read JavaScript functions and objects and to have used a command line.

modules.title: The type system
modules.description: What types are, how TypeScript infers and narrows them, and how generics and type operators describe code you have not written yet.

modules.title: The Node.js runtime
modules.description: How Node runs JavaScript outside the browser: modules, the event loop, bytes and streams, HTTP and failure handling.

modules.title: Building services
modules.description: Packages, versions and tests, and a typed service that validates what enters it and shuts down cleanly.

concepts.title: Static type
concepts.summary: A label the compiler attaches to a value or expression to check how it is used before the program runs.

concepts.title: Type erasure
concepts.summary: Annotations, interfaces and type aliases are removed when TypeScript is compiled, so none of them exist at run time.

concepts.title: Compile time and run time
concepts.summary: The checker reports mistakes before running, but by default the compiler still emits JavaScript when it finds errors.

concepts.title: The compiler
concepts.summary: tsc reads TypeScript and tsconfig.json, checks types, and writes JavaScript for the chosen target.

concepts.title: Type inference
concepts.summary: The compiler works out a type from the initial value, so annotations are needed mainly at boundaries.

concepts.title: Widening
concepts.summary: A mutable location widens a literal to its general type, so let a = 5 is number while const b = 5 has the literal type 5.

concepts.title: as const
concepts.summary: as const freezes a literal expression to its narrowest, readonly type.

concepts.title: Arrays and tuples
concepts.summary: [1, 'a'] is an array of string or number, and [string, number] is a tuple of fixed length and position types.

concepts.title: Object type
concepts.summary: An object type lists property names, their types and whether each is optional or readonly.

concepts.title: Structural typing
concepts.summary: A value fits a type when it has at least the required properties with compatible types, whatever it was declared as.

concepts.title: Excess property check
concepts.summary: A fresh object literal assigned to a type may not name properties the type lacks, though a variable holding the same object may.

concepts.title: Interface and type alias
concepts.summary: Both describe shapes; interfaces can be extended and merged, and aliases can name unions and other non-object types.

concepts.title: Union type
concepts.summary: A | B allows either type, and only operations valid for both are allowed until the value is narrowed.

concepts.title: Narrowing
concepts.summary: Control-flow analysis refines a union inside a branch from checks such as typeof x === 'string'.

concepts.title: Discriminated union
concepts.summary: A union whose members share a literal-typed property, such as kind, lets one check identify the member.

concepts.title: Exhaustiveness with never
concepts.summary: If every member is handled, the leftover type is never, and assigning it to never makes forgotten cases a compile error.

concepts.title: Type parameter
concepts.summary: A name such as T that stands in for a type and that the compiler fills in from the call, so one function can relate its input and output types.

concepts.title: Inference from the call
concepts.summary: The type argument is usually inferred from the arguments, and written explicitly only when inference cannot decide.

concepts.title: Constraint
concepts.summary: T extends Shape limits the argument to types with that shape, and lets the body use those members.

concepts.title: Generic containers
concepts.summary: Array<T>, Promise<T> and Map<K, V> are ordinary types that carry other types.

concepts.title: keyof and typeof
concepts.summary: keyof T is the union of T's property names, and typeof x takes the type of a value.

concepts.title: Indexed access
concepts.summary: T['name'] is the type of that property, and typeof arr[number] is the element type of an array type.

concepts.title: Utility types
concepts.summary: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit and Record build new object types from existing ones.

concepts.title: One source of truth
concepts.summary: Deriving types from a value or a base type keeps them from drifting apart.

concepts.title: any and unknown
concepts.summary: any switches checking off for a value, while unknown accepts anything but demands narrowing before use.

concepts.title: Type assertion
concepts.summary: value as T tells the checker to trust you, adds no run-time check and is rejected only when the types cannot overlap.

concepts.title: Unchecked index access
concepts.summary: Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, xs[0] has type number even when the array may be empty.

concepts.title: Validate at the boundary
concepts.summary: JSON.parse returns any, so input is parsed into unknown and checked by a guard or a schema library before it is typed.

concepts.title: Runtime
concepts.summary: Node packages the V8 engine with libuv's event loop, file and network APIs and a module system, so JavaScript can run outside a browser.

concepts.title: ES modules and CommonJS
concepts.summary: import/export modules are the standard, require/module.exports is the older system, and package.json type or the file extension selects which one a file is.

concepts.title: Built-in modules
concepts.summary: Built-ins such as fs and http are imported with the node: prefix, which marks them as part of the runtime rather than a package.

concepts.title: process.env
concepts.summary: Environment variables arrive as strings or undefined, so numbers and booleans must be parsed.

concepts.title: One thread of JavaScript
concepts.summary: Your code runs on one thread, so any long synchronous task delays every other callback.

concepts.title: nextTick and promises
concepts.summary: process.nextTick callbacks run first after the current operation, then promise callbacks, and both run before the loop moves on.

concepts.title: Timers and setImmediate
concepts.summary: Inside an I/O callback setImmediate always runs before a zero-delay timer, while from the main module the order is not guaranteed.

concepts.title: Offloading work
concepts.summary: I/O is performed outside the JavaScript thread, and CPU-heavy work belongs in worker threads or another process.

concepts.title: Buffer
concepts.summary: A Buffer is a fixed-size block of bytes, and text becomes bytes through an encoding such as UTF-8.

concepts.title: Characters versus bytes
concepts.summary: A string's length counts UTF-16 code units while its UTF-8 size counts bytes, and the two differ for non-ASCII text.

concepts.title: Stream
concepts.summary: A stream moves data in chunks, so a large file can be processed without holding all of it in memory.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: write() returns false when the internal buffer reaches the high-water mark, and the producer should wait for drain.

concepts.title: Request and response objects
concepts.summary: A handler receives the request (method, url, headers, a body stream) and writes a status, headers and body to the response.

concepts.title: Routing
concepts.summary: A router chooses a handler from the method and path, and req.url includes the query string unless it is parsed with URL.

concepts.title: The response contract
concepts.summary: A handler must set a status, a content-type and end the response, or the client waits until it times out.

concepts.title: Reading a body
concepts.summary: A request body arrives as chunks of bytes, which are collected, decoded and parsed, and bad JSON should return 400.

concepts.title: Promise combinators
concepts.summary: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection, allSettled always reports every outcome, race settles with the first to settle and any with the first to fulfil.

concepts.title: Sequential and parallel awaits
concepts.summary: await in a for loop runs tasks one after another, while Promise.all over started promises runs them together.

concepts.title: Unhandled rejections
concepts.summary: Since Node 15 a rejection nobody handles terminates the process with a non-zero exit code by default.

concepts.title: Cancellation
concepts.summary: An AbortController signal passed to an API lets the caller cancel the work, which rejects with an AbortError.

concepts.title: Semantic versioning
concepts.summary: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a major bump may break callers, a minor bump adds backwards-compatible features and a patch bump fixes bugs.

concepts.title: Range operators
concepts.summary: ^1.2.3 accepts 1.2.3 up to but not including 2.0.0, ~1.2.3 accepts up to but not including 1.3.0, and below 1.0.0 the caret is stricter.

concepts.title: Lockfile
concepts.summary: package-lock.json records the exact version of every dependency, and npm ci installs exactly that.

concepts.title: The built-in test runner
concepts.summary: node --test runs files that use node:test and node:assert, with describe/it blocks and strictEqual for comparisons.

concepts.title: Configuration at startup
concepts.summary: Read and validate environment variables once at startup, so a missing variable fails the process immediately instead of a request later.

concepts.title: Parse, don't assume
concepts.summary: Turn unknown input into a typed value in one place, returning a result or an error, so the rest of the code sees only valid data.

concepts.title: Graceful shutdown
concepts.summary: On SIGTERM stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources and exit.

concepts.title: Logs and health
concepts.summary: Structured logs with a request id and a health endpoint make a service operable.

lessons.title: What types are for

steps.headline: A static type is a label the compiler attaches to a value, and it checks every use of the value against that label before the program runs.

lead.text: In let n: number = 5; the part : number is an **annotation**, a note to the compiler that n is to hold numbers. From then on the compiler treats every use of n as a use of a number, and the label is called n's **static type**, static because it is fixed and checked while the code is still just text. Line 2 of the figure assigns the string "five" to n, which contradicts the label, so the compiler refuses it.

The refusal is a message, and it has the same four parts every time. The file name and position say where to look, the word *error* gives the severity, the code TS2322 is a number that can be searched for, and the sentence after it says what was wrong. Reading the sentence from left to right gives you the whole mistake: the value on the line is a string, and the place it is going to accepts only a number.

afterFigure.text: The compiler reached this conclusion without running anything. It did not need to see "five" arrive in n, because the types alone were enough to show that the assignment cannot be right, and that is the whole use of the checker: it finds a mistake of this kind on the day you type it, and not on the day a user triggers it.

diagram.alt: A two-line program, then the compiler's error report split into where, severity, code and message.
diagram.caption: The report for line 2, taken apart. Use the buttons to move between the code and the report.

reveal.text: The checker reports the line where a value contradicts a label, which is not always the line where the label was written.

lead.text: Before the next screen explains it, decide what the compiler writes for this file. The first line gives x a label, and the second describes a shape called A.

reveal.text: The next screen shows the output line by line and explains why each piece stayed or went.

steps.headline: Every annotation, interface and type alias is removed when TypeScript is compiled, so the JavaScript contains none of them.

lead.text: The compiler's output is ordinary JavaScript, and a JavaScript engine has no notion of : number, so the emitter has to leave all of it out. This is called **type erasure**. An annotation is deleted from the line it sits on, leaving the rest of the line as it was, and a declaration that exists only for the checker, such as an interface or a type alias, is deleted completely. Use the buttons to compare the file with its output.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the output keeps the function's two names, f and a, and everything that does work, such as String(a). Erasure removes labels and never changes behaviour, which is why a TypeScript program and its JavaScript output do the same thing when they run.
It also follows that a type cannot be looked at while the program runs. By the time anything executes, A and T do not exist, so there is nothing for typeof or instanceof to find.

lead.text: Erasure removes labels and leaves behaviour alone. Apply that to a function whose every parameter carries a label.

reveal.text: Names are kept because the body uses them, and only the part after each colon is dropped.

steps.headline: Compile a file with four declarations, one at a time, and work out what remains.

workedSteps.text: The first declaration is a constant with an annotation. The emitter deletes : number and keeps the rest.
The second is an interface. It describes a shape for the checker and has no value at run time, so the emitter writes nothing for it.
The third is a type alias, which is the same kind of declaration and is removed in the same way.
The fourth is a function. Its two annotations are deleted and its body is copied across.
Count the declarations that left no trace in the output. Enter that number.

lead.text: Apply what erasure removes to a test that must run later: a program declares an interface Dog and then asks whether pet instanceof Dog.

reveal.text: To check a shape at run time you have to write ordinary code that inspects the value, because the interface will not be there to do it.

lead.text: The figure on the previous screen showed a checker and an emitter side by side. Decide whether a mistake found by the first one stops the second.

reveal.text: The next screen shows the same pipeline with the option that makes the answer different.

steps.headline: By default tsc reports type errors and still writes the JavaScript, and the option noEmitOnError makes it stop writing instead.

lead.text: The checker's list of errors does not feed back into the emitter, so with default settings both stages always run. You can see this when you compile a file with the error from the first screen: the message appears, the command ends with a non-zero exit status, and the .js file is on disk all the same. A build script can therefore tell that something was wrong from the exit status, even though the output exists.

A project that wants no output from a broken build sets the compiler option noEmitOnError to true in its tsconfig.json, the file in which tsc finds the settings for a project, such as which files to compile and which JavaScript version to target. With that option set the figure changes: the error list is the same, but the emitter writes nothing.

afterFigure.text: The default exists for good reasons. During development you often want to run a half-finished change and see what it does, and the exit status still lets a build or a test pipeline refuse to continue.

lead.text: The pipeline you have just seen has one switch that decides whether an error stops the emitter. Name it.

reveal.text: In a tsconfig.json this would sit inside compilerOptions, set to true.

steps.headline: A type system catches mistakes, records what the author meant, and lets an editor help, but it does not inspect data that arrives while the program runs.

lead.text: TypeScript was announced by Microsoft in October 2012, with Anders Hejlsberg leading the language design, as a way to give JavaScript the kind of checking that larger programs need. Its types do three jobs. They catch mistakes before the program runs, as the first screen showed. They document intent, because function f(a: number): string tells a reader what goes in and what comes out without a comment. And they let an editor offer completion and renaming, because the editor can use the same labels the compiler does.

There is one thing they do not do. A type describes what the author *promises* about a value, and since the labels are erased, nothing checks the promise when a value arrives from a file, a network request or a user. Look at the figure's code: JSON.parse returns data whose shape the compiler cannot know, so it allows it to be labelled User, and the label is a promise nobody has tested.

afterFigure.text: The compiler accepted line 2 because it was told to trust the label, and the program then fails at run time on a value the label said would be there. Later lessons return to this gap, and the last two lessons close it by checking data as it enters the program.

diagram.alt: A code listing in which JSON.parse is assigned to a variable labelled User, followed by a line printing u.name, with the value undefined shown as the result.
diagram.caption: The label says User and the data says otherwise. The compiler cannot see the difference.

cases.label: What runs

lessons.orientation: Explain that types exist only at compile time, read a basic compiler error and say what the compiled JavaScript contains.
lessons.nextAction: Predict the type TypeScript infers for a declaration, including how let, const and as const change it.

blocks.text: Run this line of JavaScript, let n = 5; n = "five";, and it works without complaint, because a JavaScript variable may hold a number at one moment and a string the next. The same two lines in TypeScript, with n labelled as a number, are rejected before they ever run: error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'. The label is the whole difference, and what it costs is a second tool that reads your code before the first one runs it.

That second tool is the TypeScript compiler, tsc. The figure shows its two stages, a checker that reads the labels and reports mistakes, and an emitter that writes the JavaScript. Keeping the two apart explains most of what surprises people about TypeScript, from why a program with errors can still run to why a type can never be looked at when it does.

diagram.alt: A pipeline from a.ts through a checker and an emitter to a.js, with an error list rising from the checker.
diagram.caption: The checker and the emitter are separate stages. Use the buttons to see what each one produces.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a basic compiler error, say which parts of a TypeScript file survive into the JavaScript, and explain why types cannot check data at run time.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson in the course rests on the line between what the checker sees and what actually runs.

recap.keyIdea: Types are checked by the compiler and erased from the JavaScript it writes, so they catch mistakes before the program runs and never exist while it does.

blocks.text: You read TS2322 as a value of one type going somewhere that accepts another, and you saw that the emitter deletes annotations, interfaces and type aliases while keeping everything that does work. By default tsc reports an error and still writes the file, which noEmitOnError changes.
Because the labels are gone by run time, a type describes a promise about a value and does not inspect it, and that is why JSON.parse can hand back data that does not match the type it was given.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how the compiler works out a type for itself, so that most of your code needs no annotations at all.

lessons.title: Inference and literal types

steps.headline: The compiler works out a type from a declaration's initial value, so most code needs no annotations at all.

lead.text: Every declaration in the figure was written without a type, and each still has one. The compiler looks at the value on the right of the equals sign, sees that 5 is a number, and gives the variable that type, a process called **type inference**. Writing : number after a would add nothing, and a reader who knows the rule can read the declared type straight off the value.

Inference runs on the same rules as annotations, so an inferred type is as binding as a written one: after let a = 5; the assignment a = "five" produces the TS2322 error from the previous lesson. What inference adds is that you only have to write a type where there is no value for the compiler to learn it from, a point the last screen of this lesson returns to.
Decide what type the compiler gives b in the declaration below, before the next screen explains how let and const differ. The answer is a single number, because b never changes.

reveal.text: The next screen shows where that type sits relative to number, and why let behaves differently.

steps.headline: A const keeps the literal type of its value, while a let widens it to the general type, because only a let can change later.

lead.text: A **literal type** is a type that holds exactly one value, such as 5 or "hi". It sits below the general type in the figure, because every value of type 5 is also a number, and the compiler picks between the two according to how the variable can change. A const can never be reassigned, so the narrow type 5 is safe and is kept. A let can be assigned again, perhaps with 6 or 7, and a type of 5 would reject those, so the compiler **widens** the type to number.
The same rule applies to strings: let g = "hi" has type string, while const h = "hi" has the literal type "hi".

afterFigure.text: Widening happens once, at the declaration. If you write const day = "mon" and then let d2 = day, the second line widens again and d2 is a string, because it is a new mutable location.

diagram.alt: A column of three types: unknown at the top, number below it and the literal type 5 at the bottom. With let, an arrow rises from 5 to number. With const, the type stays at 5.
diagram.caption: A literal type sits below its general type. Use the buttons to compare let and const.

lead.text: Apply the rule to a mutable variable: the value below is a string, and the declaration uses let.

reveal.text: Had the declaration used const, the type would have been the single value "hi", written with its quotation marks.

steps.headline: Work out the type of the object below, then see how as const changes it.

workedSteps.text: The declaration is a constant holding an object with one property, kind.
The const stops d from being reassigned, but it does not stop the properties inside it from changing, so kind is a mutable location and its literal type widens.
That is why d.kind = "square" is allowed. Adding as const freezes the whole expression to its narrowest form.
The property keeps its literal type and becomes read-only, so the same assignment is now an error. Name the modifier the compiler adds to the property.

steps.headline: as const freezes an expression to its narrowest type, keeping each exact value and making every property and element read-only.

lead.text: Put as const after an object or an array literal and the compiler stops widening anywhere inside it. Each string and number keeps its exact value as a literal type, each object property becomes readonly, and an array stops being a list of any length and becomes a **tuple** of exactly the elements written, which is also read-only. The figure compares the two forms of the same two declarations.

The array case is the one used most. After const dirs = ["up", "down"] as const, the type of dirs is the readonly pair of exactly those two strings, and dirs.push("left") is rejected because a readonly tuple has no push.

afterFigure.text: A frozen array also gives you a type for free. The expression typeof dirs[number] reads as the type of any element of dirs, and for the list above it is "up" | "down", so a list of allowed values can be written once and used both as data and as a type.

diagram.alt: Two declarations and their inferred types, once without as const and once with it. Without it the object has a plain string property and the array is string[]. With it the property is readonly with a literal type and the array is a readonly tuple.
diagram.caption: as const keeps the exact values and makes them read-only. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Writing as const once is enough, because it reaches every property inside the literal.

steps.headline: A tuple type fixes both the length of an array and the type at each position, which an ordinary array type does not.

lead.text: The type (string | number)[] says that a value is an array of any length, each element being a string or a number, and it is what the compiler infers for [1, "a"]. A **tuple type** such as [string, number] says more: the array has exactly two elements, the first a string and the second a number. It suits a small record whose parts have different meanings by position.

A tuple's errors say what went wrong with the length or the order. Assigning ["a", 1, 2] to [string, number] is reported as TS2322 followed by the line Source has 3 element(s) but target allows only 2. Assigning ["a"] gives Source has 1 element(s) but target requires 2, and putting the number first reports a mismatch at each position.

afterFigure.text: Both messages are about the two things a tuple promises, how many elements there are and what each one is, so reading one tells you which promise was broken.

diagram.alt: Two slot diagrams. An array type allows any number of slots that each hold a string or a number. A tuple type has exactly two slots, the first a string and the second a number.
diagram.caption: An array describes a collection of one kind of thing. A tuple describes a fixed record by position.

cases.label: Array

lead.text: Apply both promises of a tuple, its length and the type at each position, to four different arrays, and count the ones that break either promise.

reveal.text: A function that returns a pair, such as a name and an age, can use this type, and a caller who swaps them is told at once.

steps.headline: Annotations are needed where the compiler has no value to infer from, which is mainly function parameters and empty collections.

lead.text: Inference needs a value, and a function parameter has none until someone calls the function. Given function area(r) { return r * r; } the compiler reports TS7006, Parameter 'r' implicitly has an 'any' type, because it cannot know what r will be, and the fix is to write r: number. The same applies to the parameters of any function that other code will call, so the signature of an exported function is where annotations are worth the most: they are the contract that callers are checked against.

An empty collection is the other case. The declaration const xs: number[] = [] says what the list will hold, which the empty brackets cannot. Elsewhere, a local variable with a value, such as const total = 0, is better left alone, since an annotation there only repeats what the value already says.
Decide which of these declarations the compiler could not work out for itself, using the rule that inference needs a value.

reveal.text: A rule of thumb follows: annotate the boundaries of your code, such as parameters and exports, and let inference do the rest inside.

lessons.orientation: Predict the type TypeScript infers for a declaration, including how let, const and as const change it.
lessons.nextAction: Describe an object's shape as a type and say whether a given value fits it.

blocks.text: Here are three declarations with no types written anywhere: let a = 5, const b = 5 and let c = [1, "a"]. The compiler still gives each one a type, and the three are not alike. The variable a is a number, b is the single value 5, and c is an array whose elements are strings or numbers, so the checker has read more from each declaration than the declaration says.

Knowing what it will conclude is what lets you write less. This lesson covers the rules for that, which depend on whether a value can change, and the small set of places where the compiler cannot work out a type from a value and has to be told.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict the type inferred for a declaration, say why let and const differ, and use as const and tuple types.
intro.whyItMatters: Most TypeScript you read has few annotations, so reading it means knowing what the compiler has inferred.

recap.keyIdea: The compiler infers a type from the initial value, keeping the exact value for a const and widening it for a let, and you annotate only where there is no value to learn from.

blocks.text: A const keeps the literal type of its value and a let widens it, so b is 5 while a is number, and an object property widens too unless as const freezes the expression, which also makes it readonly. A tuple fixes the length and the type at each position, and an ordinary array does not.
Annotations are worth writing at function parameters and exported signatures, and on empty collections, because those are the places where no value exists for the compiler to learn from.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson describes the shape of an object as a type and shows how the compiler decides whether a value fits it.

lessons.title: Shapes and structural typing

steps.headline: An object type lists each property with its type, and marks a property as optional with a question mark or as readonly with a modifier.

lead.text: An object type is a description of the properties a value should have. In the figure the interface Person requires a name that is a string, allows a nick that is a string, and has an id that is a number. Writing it as interface Person { name: string } and writing it inline as { name: string } describe the same shape, and the inline form is useful for a type that is used once.

A property is **optional** when its name is followed by a question mark. Reading an optional property gives its type or undefined, so with strict checking on, person.nick.length is rejected with TS18048, 'person.nick' is possibly 'undefined', until the code has checked that nick is there. A property marked **readonly** can be set when the object is created and never assigned to afterwards, and the second error you meet below is the one that enforces it.
Before the next screen explains how the compiler decides, work out whether the class Dog may be used where an interface Named is expected. Dog does not mention Named anywhere.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the rule the compiler applies and tests it against three values.

steps.headline: A value fits an object type when it has at least the required properties with compatible types, however it was declared.

lead.text: TypeScript decides whether a value fits a type by comparing shapes, a rule called **structural typing**. The target type Named asks for one thing, a property called name that holds a string, and any value that has it fits. A class instance fits, and so does a plain object, and neither had to announce a relationship with Named beforehand. This differs from languages in which a class must say that it implements an interface, and it suits JavaScript, where objects are built up from whatever properties they need.

The rule asks for *at least* the required properties. A value with extra properties still fits, because everything the target needs is present, so Dog with its bark method fits Named and a number, which has no name, does not.

afterFigure.text: This is also why types describe what code needs, not what a value is. A function that takes a Named only reads name, and it will work with every value that has one.

diagram.alt: A target type Named, which needs a name string, and three values tested against it: a class instance with an extra method, an object with extra properties, and a number. The first two fit and the number does not.
diagram.caption: Fit depends on the properties a value has. How it was declared never matters. Use the buttons to try three values.

lead.text: Apply the rule from the last screen to five values, remembering that extra properties are allowed and that the type of each property still matters.

reveal.text: The values are held in variables here. The next screen shows why that detail matters.

steps.headline: A fresh object literal assigned to a typed place may not name extra properties, though a variable holding the same object may.

lead.text: There is one exception to the rule that extra properties are harmless. When you write an object literal directly where a type is expected, as in const p: { x: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 }, the compiler checks that every property in the literal is known to the target, and reports TS2353 for y. This is the **excess property check**, and it exists to catch typos: if the target has a property called name and the literal says nam, the extra property is much more likely to be a spelling mistake than something wanted.

The check applies only to a fresh literal, meaning one written at the place of use. Put the same object in a variable first, as the second view of the figure shows, and the assignment passes, because the variable already existed and no longer looks like a typo.

afterFigure.text: It follows that the error is about the *literal*, not about the data. At run time the extra property is harmless, and the checker is guarding against a slip in the code you have just written.

diagram.alt: Two ways of giving the same object to the type { x: number }. Written directly, the extra property y is reported as an error. Held in a variable first, the same object is accepted.
diagram.caption: The check applies only where an object literal is written straight into a typed place. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Take one object to a type two ways, and check which route the compiler stops.

workedSteps.text: The target type is Named, which needs a name that is a string.
The first route writes the literal at the point of use. The literal has a property age that Named does not list, so the excess check reports it.
workedSteps.math: const a: Named = { name: "a", age: 3 };   error TS2353

workedSteps.text: The second route puts the same object in a variable first. The variable is not fresh, so only the shape is compared, and it has a name that is a string.
workedSteps.math:
const v = { name: "a", age: 3 };
const b: Named = v;   no error

workedSteps.text: A third line writes a fresh literal with just the one required property. Count the lines of the three that report an error.

steps.headline: readonly stops assignment only in the checker, because it is erased, and an optional property adds undefined to what you read.

lead.text: Both modifiers are enforced at the same moment as every other type rule, which is when the code is checked. With interface P { readonly x: number }, the line p.x = 2 is rejected with TS2540, Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property. The compiled JavaScript contains no trace of the modifier, so it is a promise about the code you have written and does not protect the object while the program runs.

An optional property is a promise of a different kind. The type of nick in the previous figure is string | undefined, so you may leave it out when creating the object and you must deal with its absence when reading it. A line such as const m: Person = { name: "a", id: 1 } is fine, and a read of m.nick that assumes a string is the error from the first screen.
Apply the modifier to five lines in which one property can be set once and the other can be set freely.

reveal.text: The checker sees the assignment and never the run-time value, so the error appears while you are typing and not when the code runs.

steps.headline: Interfaces and type aliases both describe object shapes, but an interface can be extended and merged, and an alias can also name unions and other types.

lead.text: For describing an object the two are nearly interchangeable. interface Child extends Base { name: string } adds a property to an existing shape, and an alias reaches the same result with an intersection, which later lessons cover. An interface has one extra ability, which is that two declarations of the same name are merged into one type, as the first view of the figure shows. An alias has the opposite rule, and a repeated name is an error.

An alias can name things that an interface cannot, such as the union type U = string | number, and that is the next lesson's subject. A sensible default is to use an interface for an object shape that may be extended and an alias for everything else, and to follow whatever a project already does.

afterFigure.text: Neither survives compilation, so the choice affects only how you write types and what the checker reports, and never what runs.

diagram.alt: An interface declared twice is merged into one type with both properties. A type alias declared twice is an error.
diagram.caption: Declaring the same name twice. Use the buttons to compare an interface and a type alias.

cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 246"><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="30" width="592" height="92" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="66" text-anchor="start">type T = { a: number };</text><text class="t-small" x="44" y="100" text-anchor="start">type T = { b: number };</text><rect class="f-warn-soft s-warn w3" x="24" y="146" width="592" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="177" text-anchor="start">Error TS2300: Duplicate identifier T.</text></svg>

lead.text: Carry the structural rule over to declarations: two declarations with the same name are written one after the other, once with each keyword.

reveal.text: Merging is useful for adding to a type that a library declared, which is how many libraries are extended.

lessons.orientation: Decide whether a value fits an object type by its shape, and predict when excess property checks and readonly stop an assignment.
lessons.nextAction: Write a union type and narrow it with a check so that each branch knows what it holds.

blocks.text: Suppose a function takes a Named, which is an interface with a single property, name, that holds a string. A class Dog, written earlier by someone who has never heard of Named, has a name property and a method called bark. TypeScript accepts a Dog wherever a Named is expected, with no declaration connecting the two, because it compares what each one has and finds everything that Named asks for.

That comparison is the idea behind most of the errors you will read about objects. The figure picks out the three kinds of property an object type can list, and the rest of the lesson shows how the compiler decides that a value fits, and the two situations in which it is stricter than that.

diagram.caption: One type, three kinds of property. Use the buttons to pick out each kind.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a value fits an object type by its shape, and predict when an extra property or a readonly assignment is reported.
intro.whyItMatters: Most errors about objects come down to a missing property, an unknown one or a readonly one.

recap.keyIdea: A value fits an object type by its shape, so extra properties are allowed, except on a fresh literal, and readonly is enforced only by the checker.

blocks.text: The compiler compares the properties a value has with the properties a type requires, so a class instance fits an interface it never mentions, and extra properties do no harm. The exception is a fresh object literal, where an unknown property is reported as a probable typo, and the same object held in a variable passes.

A readonly property rejects assignment at check time only, because the modifier is erased, and an optional property adds undefined to what you read. An interface can be extended and merged, and an alias can also name unions.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at unions, which let a value be one of several types, and at how the compiler narrows them as your code checks which one it holds.

lessons.title: Unions and narrowing

steps.headline: A union type allows a value to be one of several types, and the checker permits only the operations that are valid for every member.

lead.text: A **union type** is written with a vertical bar, so string | number describes a value that is a string or a number. The checker does not know which, and it takes the careful view: an operation is allowed only if it is valid whichever member the value turns out to be. In function f(x: string | number), the expression x.length is rejected with TS2339, Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number', and the line beneath explains that the property is missing on type 'number'.

Operations that both members have are fine, such as x.toString(), because every string and every number has one. The error does not say that x is wrong. It says that the code has not yet found out which type x has, and the next screens show how code can find out.
Decide how many of the three method calls below the checker allows on a value that is a string or a number. The previous screen gave the rule, and the answer depends on which methods both types have.

reveal.text: The rule is a safe one, and the next screen shows how code can unlock the other operations by finding out which type it holds.

steps.headline: A check on the value narrows a union inside the branch it guards, so each branch sees only the members that can still occur.

lead.text: The figure follows x through the function from the start of the lesson. At the top it may be a string or a number. The test typeof x === "string" can only be true for a string, so inside the branch the checker removes number, and x.length is allowed. The branch returns, so after the if the string case has been dealt with and only number is left, and x.toFixed(1) is allowed. This process is called **narrowing**, and the checker follows it through the code without any annotation from you.

The checks that narrow are ordinary run-time tests: typeof, comparison with null or another value, and the in operator, which asks whether an object has a property. The second figure shows three of them. Narrowing works because the test really runs, so a check on the value is trusted, and an annotation or an as cast, which only tells the checker what to believe, does not narrow anything.

afterFigure.text: That is why narrowing is reliable. The condition that protects a branch is the same condition that runs, so the branch cannot be reached with the wrong type.

diagram.alt: Three checks that narrow a union. Each leaves some members of the union lit: typeof removes one kind of primitive, equality with null removes null, and the in operator keeps the members that have a property.
diagram.caption: Each check removes members from the union. Use the buttons to see three checks.

reveal.text: The checker did this with no annotation. In an editor, hovering x on the last line would show boolean.

steps.headline: A union whose members share a literal-typed property lets one check on that property identify the member.

lead.text: Real unions are usually of object types. Suppose a Shape is a circle with a radius r, a rectangle with a width w and a height h, or a triangle with a base b and a height h, and that each carries a property kind holding the literal "circle", "rect" or "tri". A property like kind is called a **discriminant**, and a union with one is a **discriminated union**: a check on it tells the compiler which member it holds.

In a switch (s.kind), each case narrows s to the single member whose kind matches, as the figure shows. Outside the matching case, s.r is an error, because a rectangle has no radius, and TS2339 says that the property does not exist on the type Shape. Inside case "circle" the same expression is fine.

afterFigure.text: The literal types from the second lesson are what make this work. Had kind been typed as a plain string, a check of its value could not tell the members apart.

diagram.alt: A Shape union with three members, circle, rect and tri. In each view a case of a switch on s.kind is chosen and only the matching member stays lit.
diagram.caption: Checking the kind picks one member. Use the buttons to move between the cases.

steps.headline: Assigning the leftover value to never in a default branch turns a forgotten case into a compile error that names it.

lead.text: After every member of a union has been handled, the checker has nothing left to say about the value, and the type that remains is **never**, the type with no values. A default branch can be used to check this. Writing default: const _x: never = s; compiles only if every kind has been handled before it. If the tri case is missing, the leftover type is the tri member, and TS2322 says that the type with kind "tri" is not assignable to type never, which names the shape that was forgotten.

The reasoning is the reverse of what a default branch usually does. A catch-all default returns something for new members and hides them, whereas the never check refuses to compile until someone has decided what each new member should do. Later, when a fourth shape is added to the union, every switch written this way will report it.

afterFigure.text: The check costs one line and has no effect at run time, because the type is erased and the line is never reached when the cases are complete.

steps.headline: An optional parameter is a union with undefined, so it must be narrowed or accessed with ?. before its properties are used.

lead.text: A parameter written name?: string has the type string | undefined, which is a union like the others, and the same rule applies. In function greet(name?: string) { return name.toUpperCase(); } the compiler reports TS18048, 'name' is possibly 'undefined', and the program really would crash on greet(), with a TypeError at run time. The first way to deal with it is to narrow, with if (name !== undefined) or if (name), and the second is the **optional chaining** operator ?., which stops and gives undefined when what is on its left is undefined or null.

The third apparent way is the non-null assertion name!.toUpperCase(), which silences the error by telling the checker to trust you. It compiles to name.toUpperCase(), so the crash is still there, as a later lesson explains.
Run the optional chaining operator in your head on a value that is missing.

reveal.text: The result is itself undefined, so the code that uses it must handle that, for example with a default value.

lessons.orientation: Narrow a union with typeof, in, equality and discriminant checks, and use never to prove a switch is exhaustive.
lessons.nextAction: Write a generic function and say what type the compiler infers for it from a call.

blocks.text: Calling x.length on a value typed string | number is an error, TS2339, and the reason is not that x is wrong. The checker knows only that x is a string or a number, and a number has no length, so the safe course is to refuse until the code has found out which. A test such as typeof x === "string" finds out, and the figure shows what the checker does with the answer: inside the test x is a string, and after it, x is a number.

That one mechanism covers most of what you do with unions, from a function that accepts several kinds of input to a result that is either a value or an error. The lesson follows it from typeof to objects with a kind property, and ends with a check that makes the compiler list the cases you forgot.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to narrow a union with a check, predict the type in each branch, and use never to prove that every case is handled.
intro.whyItMatters: Unions are how TypeScript describes data that can take several forms, which is most real data.

recap.keyIdea: A check on a value narrows a union to the members that can still occur, and assigning the leftover to never proves that every member has been handled.

blocks.text: A union allows only the operations that every member supports, and a run-time check such as typeof, a comparison or a literal kind narrows it inside the branch it guards. A shared literal property makes an object union discriminated, so a switch on it narrows each case to one member.

After all members are handled the leftover type is never, so a default branch that assigns to never fails to compile when a case is missing, and an optional value is a union with undefined that needs a check or ?. before use.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes types that take a type as a parameter, so that one function can work for strings, numbers or shapes and still keep track of which.

lessons.title: Generics

steps.headline: A type parameter is a name such as T that stands for a type chosen by each call, so a function can tie its output to its input.

lead.text: Take a function that returns the first element of a list. Written for numbers it has the signature (xs: number[]) => number | undefined, and for strings it would have to be written again. Giving the parameter type any[] and the result type any avoids the repetition, but it throws away what the compiler knew: in the figure with any, the call a.toUpperCase() is accepted although a is a number, and the program crashes when it runs.

A **type parameter** solves this. In function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined the T in angle brackets declares a name, and the compiler fills it in again at every call, so that the type of the input list and the type of the result are the same T. A function written this way is called **generic**. Unlike any, T *keeps the relationship*: whatever goes in as the element type comes out as the result type.

afterFigure.text: The T is like a function parameter, but for a type. It exists only while the checker is working, and it is erased with all the other types when the code is compiled.

diagram.alt: Two versions of a function that returns the first element. With any, the result is any and a nonsense method call is accepted. With a type parameter, the result is number or undefined and the same call is rejected.
diagram.caption: Both functions do the same thing at run time. Use the buttons to compare what the checker knows.

lead.text: Use the signature above to decide the type of the value that comes back from first([1, 2]), before the next screen explains how the compiler arrives at T.

reveal.text: The next screen shows where T comes from, and the figure has three more calls to compare.

steps.headline: The compiler infers T from the arguments of the call, and you write it explicitly only where the arguments cannot decide.

lead.text: Nothing in the call first([1, 2]) says what T is, and nothing has to, because the compiler looks at the argument. The list has two numbers, so T is number, and the signature then gives the result type as number | undefined. With first(["a", 1]) the elements are of two kinds, so T is the union string | number. With an empty list, first([]), there is nothing to learn from and the result is just undefined.

A function may have more than one type parameter. In function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] the two are filled in independently, so pair("x", 1) has the type [string, number], as the figure shows. When inference cannot decide, you can write the type argument yourself, as in wrap<string>("a"), and the compiler then checks the argument against it.

afterFigure.text: Reading a generic signature is therefore a matter of substitution: replace each type parameter with what the call supplies, and read the signature as an ordinary one.

steps.headline: Read the signature of pair, then work out the type of a call.

workedSteps.text: The signature declares its type parameters between angle brackets, right after the name.
workedSteps.math: function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B]

workedSteps.text: There are two type parameters, A and B, and each is used for one value parameter.
workedSteps.math: A for a, B for b

workedSteps.text: For the call pair("x", 1), the first argument is a string, so A is string, and the second is a number, so B is number.
Substitute into the return type, which is a tuple of the two.

steps.headline: T extends Shape limits the arguments to types with that shape, and lets the body use the members the constraint guarantees.

lead.text: A bare T could be any type at all, so the body of a generic function may not assume anything about it. In function longest<T>(a: T, b: T) { return a.length >= b.length ? a : b; } the reads of length are rejected, because T might be a number. The remedy is a **constraint**: T extends { length: number } says that T may be any type that has at least a numeric length property, by the same rule of shape that governed assignment earlier.

A constraint works in both directions. Inside the function, a.length is now allowed, because every possible T has it. At each call, the argument is checked against the constraint, so longest("ab", "c") and longest([1], [2, 3]) are accepted and longest(1, 2) is rejected with TS2345, Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type '{ length: number; }'.

afterFigure.text: One more detail: both parameters share the single T, so the two arguments must agree. In longest("ab", [1]) the compiler takes T from the first argument and rejects the array.

diagram.alt: The function longest, whose type parameter must have a numeric length property, with three calls. A string pair and an object with length are accepted, and a pair of numbers is rejected.
diagram.caption: The constraint T extends { length: number } filters what T may be. Use the buttons to try three calls.

cases.label: Two strings

lead.text: Apply both rules from the last screen to five calls: every argument must have a numeric length, and both arguments must agree on a single type.

reveal.text: The second rule is a consequence of using T twice, and a signature with two parameters, T and U, would accept the mixed pair.

steps.headline: Array<T>, Promise<T> and Map<K, V> are ordinary generic types, and await turns a Promise<T> into a T.

lead.text: The generics you write follow the same pattern as types you have already met. number[] is shorthand for Array<number>, a Map that maps strings to numbers is Map<string, number>, and a function that will deliver a number later returns a Promise<number>. In each, the angle brackets say which type the container holds, so that m.get("a") has the type number | undefined, because a key may be missing.

The case you meet most is the Promise. An async function always returns a Promise, so async function load(): Promise<number> returns a Promise<number> when it is called, and await load() unwraps that to the number inside. The compiler tracks the unwrapping for you, which is why writing await removes the Promise from the type.

afterFigure.text: Like any type parameter, the one inside Promise<number> is erased. At run time there is only a Promise, and nothing records that it was meant to hold a number.

diagram.alt: Three generic container types, Array of T, Promise of T and Map of K and V, each carrying another type, and an await that turns Promise of number into number.
diagram.caption: Containers are ordinary generic types. Use the buttons to compare three of them.

lead.text: Follow the type through an await, from the declared return type of the function to the variable that receives the value.

reveal.text: Without await, v would be the Promise itself, and calling a number method on it would be an error.

lead.text: Combine generics with the literal rule from the second lesson: the identity function returns whatever type it is given, and the call passes a literal into a const.

reveal.text: The literal-versus-general rule from the second lesson applies to inferred type arguments exactly as it does to declarations.

lessons.orientation: Read a generic signature, predict the type argument TypeScript infers, and constrain a type parameter so only valid arguments are accepted.
lessons.nextAction: Derive a type from another type or from a value with keyof, indexed access and utility types.

blocks.text: Consider a function that returns the first element of a list. If it takes a list of any kind and returns any, it works for every list and tells the compiler nothing, so first([1, 2]).toUpperCase() passes the check and then crashes. If it is written once for each element type, the checker knows everything and the code is repeated for numbers, strings and every type that comes after.

A **type parameter** gives the function a name for the type it is working with, so that it is written once and each call fills in the type. The figure shows the idea on first, and by the end of the lesson you will be able to read a signature such as <T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T) and say what each call to it produces.

diagram.alt: A generic function first with one type parameter T. A call goes in on the left, T is filled in by the compiler in the middle, and the result type comes out on the right.
diagram.caption: One function, and T filled in differently for each call. Use the buttons to try three calls.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a generic signature, predict the type argument the compiler infers from a call, and constrain a type parameter.
intro.whyItMatters: Libraries are written with generics, so reading their signatures depends on it.

recap.keyIdea: A type parameter is filled in by each call, so a generic function keeps the relationship between its input and output types, and a constraint says what a type must have.

blocks.text: A type parameter such as T names a type that the compiler infers from the arguments at each call, which lets first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined return number | undefined for a list of numbers. Unlike any it keeps the link between input and output, and it is erased like every other type.

A constraint such as T extends { length: number } rejects arguments without the required members and allows the body to use them. Array, Map and Promise are generic types too, and await turns a Promise<T> into a T.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson builds new types from existing ones, with keyof, indexed access and the utility types, so that a type is written once and the rest follow from it.

lessons.title: Transforming types

steps.headline: keyof T is the union of T's property names, and typeof applied to a value gives the type that value has.

lead.text: A program often needs a type that follows from something already written, and two operators produce one. The operator **keyof** takes a type and gives the union of its property names as string literals, so for { id: number; name: string; email?: string } the result is "id" | "name" | "email". A variable of that type can hold exactly those three strings, and the compiler rejects any other, which makes it a safe type for a function that takes the name of a field.

The operator **typeof**, used in a type position, takes a value and gives its type, as in type Point = typeof origin. It is different from the typeof you use in a branch, which produces a string at run time: in a type position it is erased with everything else, and it only reads the type the checker already holds for the value.

diagram.alt: Two ways of reading a type from existing code. keyof U gives the union of the property names of U. typeof applied to a value gives the type of that value.
diagram.caption: keyof works on a type and typeof works on a value. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: The operator keyof turns the property names of a type into a union. Decide how many members that union has for the type below, before the next screen introduces the operator by name.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the operator its name and puts a second, related one beside it.

lead.text: Apply keyof to a type with three properties and test four strings against it, one of which differs only in a capital letter.

reveal.text: This is the type to use for a function that takes the name of a field, because a typo is caught where it is written.

steps.headline: T["name"] is the type of that property, and indexing an array type by number gives the type of its elements.

lead.text: Square brackets in a type read a property's type from another type. With U["name"] the result is string, and with U["email"] it is string | undefined, because an optional property may be missing. The key inside the brackets is itself a type, so it can be a union: U["id" | "name"] is number | string.

The same notation works on arrays, where the key type is number. If dirs is the frozen array from the second lesson, typeof dirs[number] reads as the type of any element of the type of dirs, which is "up" | "down". Together with keyof, it lets you take a type apart: U[keyof U] is the union of every property's type in U.

diagram.alt: Looking up a property type with square brackets. U[name] is string, U[email] is string or undefined, and an array type indexed by number gives its element type.
diagram.caption: T[K] reads the type of a property. Use the buttons to try three lookups.

lead.text: Look up the type of an optional property with the square bracket notation, remembering what a missing property gives when it is read.

reveal.text: A lookup on a required property such as name has no undefined in it.

steps.headline: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit and Record are built into TypeScript, and each derives a new object type from an existing one.

lead.text: Most derived types are needed so often that they are in the language. Partial<U> makes every property optional, which suits the body of an update request in which any field may be sent. Required<U> does the opposite, so that with const b: Required<U> = { id: 1, name: "a" } the compiler reports TS2741, Property 'email' is missing. Readonly<U> makes every property readonly. The first figure shows what Partial, Required, Pick and Omit do to the same U.

Pick<U, "id" | "name"> keeps only the named properties, and Omit<U, "id"> removes them. Record<"x" | "y", number> builds an object type with one property for each key in the union, so an object that gives only x is missing y. Two limits are worth knowing: these types change only the top-level properties, so Partial<Nested> does not make the properties of a nested object optional, and Omit does not check that its keys exist, as the second figure shows.

afterFigure.text: Since Pick does check its keys, Pick<U, Exclude<keyof U, "id">> is a stricter way to write what Omit does, though Omit is what most code uses.

diagram.alt: Two derived types that name a key U does not have. Pick with the key typo is an error, while Omit with the same key typo compiles without complaint.
diagram.caption: Only Pick checks that its keys exist. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Choose a derived type for each need from a User type with id, name and an optional email.

workedSteps.text: The body of an update request may contain any field or none, so every property has to be optional.
A list view needs only the id and the name, and the compiler should check that both exist.
A form that creates a user has no id yet, because the server assigns it, so it needs everything except id.
The last type has two properties left, name and the optional email. Enter how many properties Omit<User, "id"> has.

lead.text: Recall the utility type that turns each property into an optional one, such as the body of a PATCH request needs.

reveal.text: Only the top-level properties change. A nested object's properties keep their original markers.

steps.headline: Deriving a type from a value or from a base type keeps the two in step, so that a change is made once.

lead.text: The same operators give a safe way to turn a list of allowed values into a type. Given const Color = { Red: "red", Blue: "blue" } as const, typeof Color is the object's frozen type, keyof typeof Color is the union of its keys, "Red" | "Blue", and indexing the type by those keys gives its values: type Color = typeof Color[keyof typeof Color] is "red" | "blue". The figure follows the chain, and the result is that const d: Color = "green" is an error.

This is the point of the whole lesson. The object is the single place where the allowed colors are written, and both the data and the type come from it, so adding a third entry changes the type without a second edit. The same holds when a derived type comes from a base type: whenever the base changes, everything derived from it follows.

afterFigure.text: Writing the union by hand beside the object would work today and fail quietly the first time one of the two was edited without the other.

diagram.alt: Four stages of deriving a type from a value: the object, its type, the union of its keys, and the union of its values.
diagram.caption: Each stage builds on the last. Use the buttons to move along the chain.

lessons.nextAction: Explain why any hides mistakes, use unknown safely, and say what an assertion does and does not do.

blocks.text: A project starts with a User type that has an id, a name and an optional email. Within a few weeks it also has a type for the create form, which has no id, a type for an update request, in which every field is optional, and a list type with the id and name only. Each began as a copy of User, and each now has to be edited whenever User is, which in practice means that sooner or later one of them is not.

A derived type never goes out of date, because it is defined by the type it came from. The figure applies four of the utility types that TypeScript provides to the same User, and the lesson then shows the two operators underneath them, keyof and indexed access, and how to take a type from a value.

diagram.alt: A base type U with id, name and an optional email, and the property list that results from four utility types: Partial, Required, Pick and Omit.
diagram.caption: Four new types from one base. Use the buttons to apply each one to the same U.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use keyof, indexed access and the common utility types to derive one type from another, and say what each one accepts.
intro.whyItMatters: Derived types remove the copies of a type that drift apart as a project grows.

recap.keyIdea: A type can be derived from another type or from a value, so that it is written once and every other type follows when it changes.

blocks.text: The operator keyof gives the union of a type's property names, typeof in a type position gives the type of a value, and square brackets look up a property's type. The utility types Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit and Record are built on these and change only a type's top level.

Omit does not check its keys, and Pick does, so Pick is the safer choice when the keys must exist. A frozen object, typeof, keyof and an index together turn a list of values into a union that cannot differ from the data.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the edge of the type system, where data arrives that the compiler cannot see, and at the types any and unknown.

lessons.title: Types at the edges

steps.headline: Data that enters from a file, a network or a user carries no types, and JSON.parse returns any, which switches checking off.

lead.text: A type is a promise the author makes about a value, and the checker holds the author to it inside the program. Where a value comes from outside, from a file, a request or a form, there is nobody to hold to anything, because the data is whatever it happens to be. The function JSON.parse shows the difficulty: the compiler cannot know what the text contains, so its result has the type **any**, which means that every check is switched off for that value.

The figure shows what follows. With any, the line j.anything.at.all compiles, because the checker has stopped looking, and the program fails when it runs, since j has no property called anything. The checker was not wrong. It was told to stop, and the failure appears at a distance from the place where the bad data came in.

afterFigure.text: The same applies to a request body, a configuration file and anything else that was written by another program or by a person. The way to stay safe is to treat all of it as untrusted until it has been checked.

diagram.alt: Two lines that read a property of data returned by JSON.parse. When it is typed any, an invented property is accepted. When it is typed unknown, the same line is an error.
diagram.caption: The same line against any and unknown. Use the buttons to compare.

The checker has stopped looking at j.</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="44" y="203" text-anchor="start">At run time this crashes, because j.anything is undefined.</text></svg>

cases.label: unknown
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 246"><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="30" width="592" height="92" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="66" text-anchor="start">const u: unknown = JSON.parse('{}');</text><text class="t-small" x="44" y="100" text-anchor="start">const n: number = u.anything;</text><rect class="f-warn-soft s-warn w3" x="24" y="146" width="592" height="78" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="177" text-anchor="start">TS18046: u is of type unknown.</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="44" y="203" text-anchor="start">Narrow u with a check before you use it.</text></svg>

lead.text: The parameter below is typed unknown, a type that accepts any value. Decide how many of the four statements the checker allows, before the next screen explains the rule.

reveal.text: The next screen states the rule and shows why unknown is the right type for data from outside.

steps.headline: unknown accepts any value but allows nothing to be done with it until a check has narrowed it, which makes it the safe type for outside data.

lead.text: The type **unknown** is the safe counterpart of any. Every value may be assigned to it, so it can receive the result of JSON.parse just as any does, but it allows no property access, no call and no assignment to a more specific type until the code has proved what the value is. The same line that compiled with any, u.anything, is rejected with TS18046, 'u' is of type 'unknown'.

The fix is the narrowing from the unions lesson. A check such as typeof input === "string" runs at run time and narrows input to string inside the branch, so the work that needs a string is allowed there and nowhere else. The choice between the two types is therefore easy to state: any tells the checker to stop, and unknown tells it that the value is not yet trusted.
Pick the type that makes the checker insist on a check at the boundary of a program, where JSON.parse hands over data.

reveal.text: Newer code can write JSON.parse(text) as unknown to start from the safe type.

steps.headline: An assertion with as tells the checker what to believe, adds no check at run time, and never converts a value.

lead.text: The as keyword is often used as if it converted a value, and it does not. value as T tells the checker to treat value as a T, and it compiles to just value, with nothing added and nothing changed. The checker refuses an assertion only when the two types cannot overlap, which is why "5" as number is rejected with TS2352, and the message itself suggests the way round it: convert through unknown first.

Doing so, "5" as unknown as number, compiles, and the figure's second view shows the result: at run time the value is still the string "5", and typeof reports string. The compiler now believes that t is a number, which is wrong, and every later line that uses it as one will be checked against the false belief.

afterFigure.text: An assertion is sometimes the right tool, for example where you know something the checker cannot. Where the value comes from outside, a check is the honest alternative, since it makes the belief true.

diagram.alt: Two assertions of a string to number. A direct assertion is rejected because string and number do not overlap. An assertion through unknown is accepted, and the value is still a string when the program runs.
diagram.caption: An assertion changes what the checker believes and nothing else. Use the buttons to compare.

cases.label: as unknown as number
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 246"><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="30" width="592" height="92" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="66" text-anchor="start">const t = "5" as unknown as number;</text><text class="t-small" x="44" y="100" text-anchor="start">console.log(typeof t);   // string</text><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w3" x="24" y="146" width="592" height="78" rx="8"/><text class="t-small" x="44" y="177" text-anchor="start">Accepted. At run time t is still the string "5".</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="44" y="203" text-anchor="start">The checker was told to believe it, and the value was not changed.</text></svg>

lead.text: Run the assertion in your head after erasure, when only the value and the typeof test are left.

reveal.text: The compiler's belief and the value now disagree, which is the situation validation exists to prevent.

steps.headline: By default xs[0] has the element type even when the array is empty, and the option noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to every index read.

lead.text: Reading by index is another place where a promise goes unchecked. With const xs: number[] = [], the expression xs[0] has the type number by default, although there is no element, and the program gets undefined at run time. The checker cannot know the length of an ordinary array, and by default it assumes that every index is in range.

The compiler option **noUncheckedIndexedAccess** changes that. With it on, xs[0] is number | undefined, and code has to check before using the result, as it does for any other possibly missing value. The option is not part of the strict group, so it has to be turned on in tsconfig.json by name. Strict mode checks types, and it does not check bounds.

afterFigure.text: Reading an element of a tuple at a position that exists is unaffected, because its length is part of its type.

diagram.alt: Reading the first element of an empty array of numbers. By default the type of the result is number. With the option noUncheckedIndexedAccess, it is number or undefined.
diagram.caption: The same read under two compiler settings. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Apply the option to an empty array and decide what type the compiler gives the first element.

reveal.text: Without the option, the same line would give plain number, and the program would still get undefined at run time.

steps.headline: satisfies checks a value against a type without replacing the type the compiler inferred for it.

lead.text: An annotation is a blunt instrument for checking an object. In const cfg: { port: number | string } = { port: 3000 }, the annotation makes cfg.port a string | number, although the compiler had seen that the value is 3000, and later code has to narrow it again. The operator **satisfies** keeps the check and drops the replacement: { port: 3000 } satisfies { port: number | string } fails if the object has the wrong shape, and the inferred type of port stays number.

It is therefore the better choice for a constant such as configuration, which you want to check against a type and then use with the precise types it was written with. It also reports a typo in the same way an annotation does, so { prot: 3000 } satisfies { port: number } is an error.

diagram.alt: Two ways of checking an object against a type. With satisfies, the property port keeps its own type, number. With an annotation, port takes the wider type string or number.
diagram.caption: satisfies checks without widening. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The annotation form would have given string | number, so later code would have to narrow it again.

blocks.text: Run JSON.parse('{}') and the compiler gives the result the type any, so that j.anything.at.all passes the check and then stops the program with a TypeError. The check was never going to catch it, because any is the type that tells it to look away, and JSON.parse has to return it: the text could hold anything at all.

Everything that comes into a program from outside has the same problem, and so the types you have learned so far reach only as far as the data that was already typed. The figure shows the edge of that region. This lesson covers how to cross it safely, with unknown and checks, what an assertion does and does not do, and two features that tighten the checker where it was loose.

diagram.alt: A boundary between outside data and typed code. Validated: a payload with port as a string stops at a validator. Asserted: the same payload goes around the validator on a dashed route labelled no check.
diagram.caption: The same bad payload by two routes. Use the buttons to follow each.
