intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to explain why outside data is untyped, choose unknown over any, and say what an assertion, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and satisfies each do.
intro.whyItMatters: Most real bugs in typed code enter at the edge, where a value is believed to be something it is not.

recap.keyIdea: Types cannot check data from outside, so treat it as unknown and narrow it with real checks, because an assertion only changes what the checker believes.

blocks.text: JSON.parse returns any, which switches checking off, so outside data is better held as unknown, which permits nothing until a check has narrowed it. An assertion with as is erased and never converts a value, so a wrong one hides a bug until run time, as when a port arrives as the string "80".

Strict mode does not check array bounds, and noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to every index read when you turn it on. The operator satisfies checks an object against a type and keeps the type the compiler inferred.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson leaves types for the program that runs the JavaScript, and shows what Node is made of and how it loads modules.

lessons.title: What Node is

steps.headline: Node is the V8 engine plus an event loop, file and network APIs and a module system, so that JavaScript can run outside a browser.

lead.text: JavaScript the language is the same in a browser and in Node, and what differs is the layer beneath it, shown in the figure. A browser gives your code a page to work with, through window, document and the DOM, and a program on a web page cannot read a file on the disk. **Node** is a program that embeds Google's V8 engine, the one in Chrome, and adds the platform for working outside a page: fs for files, http for servers, process for the running program and its environment, and the event loop that makes all of them asynchronous.

Because the layers differ, so do the globals. In Node, typeof window and typeof document are both "undefined", and typeof process is "object". Some names, such as fetch and the timer functions, exist on both platforms, since both have chosen to provide them. Ryan Dahl presented Node in 2009 as a way to write network programs in JavaScript without blocking on every request, an idea the event loop lesson takes up.
Decide which of four common names exist in Node, using the picture of the layers: what does the platform layer provide to a program with no page?

reveal.text: A program that needs both environments has to check for the name first, for example with typeof window.

lead.text: Node supports two module systems. Decide what typeof gives for the name __dirname in a file run as an ES module, before the next screen sets the two side by side.

reveal.text: The next screen sets the two module systems side by side and says how Node chooses between them.

steps.headline: ES modules use import and export, CommonJS uses require and module.exports, and a package.json type field or a file extension chooses between them.

lead.text: Node has two module systems because it had one before the language did. **CommonJS**, the original, uses require to load a module and module.exports to share one, and it supplies each file with __dirname and __filename. **ES modules**, the standard that came with the language, use import and export, and allow await at the top level of a file, but they get none of Node's extra names. In an ES module typeof require and typeof __dirname are both "undefined", and the file's folder is import.meta.dirname.

Node decides by looking at the file. A .mjs file is an ES module and a .cjs file is CommonJS, and for a .js file the nearest package.json decides, with "type": "module" selecting ES modules and "type": "commonjs" the other. TypeScript projects usually choose the ES module form, since it is the one the language itself defines.

afterFigure.text: The two can load each other with some care, but mixing them in one file is an error, so pick one per file and follow the package's setting.

diagram.alt: A table comparing CommonJS and ES modules by syntax, whether __dirname exists, whether top-level await is allowed, and how Node decides which one a file is.

reveal.text: import.meta.filename is the matching replacement for __filename.

steps.headline: Built-in modules are imported with the node: prefix, which marks a name as part of Node and not a package.

lead.text: Every import specifier is one of three kinds, and Node reads the form to decide where to look. A path that starts with a dot, such as ./util.js, is a file of your own. A bare name, such as express, is a package, searched for in the node_modules folders. And a name that starts with node:, such as node:fs/promises, is a built-in module that comes with Node, so no package is involved and nothing can be installed in its place.

The prefix is not strictly required for the older names, because fs alone also works, but writing it is the safer habit. It tells a reader at a glance that the import is part of the platform, and it prevents a package of the same name in node_modules from standing in for the built-in. The figure shows one specifier of each kind.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of module specifier and where Node looks for each: a node: name is a built-in module, a bare name is an installed package, and a relative path is a file.
diagram.caption: Where an import is found from. Use the buttons to try three specifiers.

lead.text: Assign a number to an entry of process.env and ask what type is stored, before the next screen describes how configuration reaches a Node program.

reveal.text: The next screen explains why this happens and how a program should read configuration.

steps.headline: Environment variables arrive as strings or undefined, so a program must parse numbers and booleans and supply a default for a missing one.

lead.text: Configuration reaches a Node program through the operating system as environment variables, which are text. process.env.PORT is therefore the string "8080" when the variable is set and **undefined** when it is not, and never a number. The program has to convert the value itself, with Number(process.env.PORT), and it has to decide what to do when nothing is there, because Number(undefined) is NaN.

The usual form is Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), where the operator ?? supplies 3000 when the left side is undefined or null. The same care applies to flags. Setting process.env.FLAG = false stores the string "false", which is truthy, so a test for a flag has to compare the text, for example with === "true".

afterFigure.text: A value that is converted once, at startup, is also easier to check. The last lesson of this course shows how to read all configuration in one place and stop early when it is wrong.

diagram.alt: Reading the environment variable PORT in three situations. When it is set to 8080 the value is the string 8080. When it is missing the value is undefined. When it is set to nothing the value is an empty string.

lead.text: Run a line that reads a port with a default, on a machine where the variable has not been set.

reveal.text: Without the ?? default, Number(undefined) would be NaN, and the server would try to listen on a port called NaN.

lead.text: Change the case from the last screen: the variable is set, but to an empty value, as a shell does when you write PORT= with nothing after the sign.

reveal.text: Which operator to use, ?? or ||, depends on whether an empty value should count as missing, and a deliberate choice avoids this surprise.

lessons.orientation: Describe what Node adds to the JavaScript engine, choose between ES modules and CommonJS, and read configuration from environment variables safely.
lessons.nextAction: Predict the order in which timers, promises and nextTick callbacks run, and what blocks the event loop.

blocks.text: Open a browser's console and type document, and you get the page. Run the same word in Node and you get a ReferenceError, since a Node program has no page. Type require or process instead and the positions reverse: a browser reports that it has never heard of them. Both are running JavaScript, by way of the same kind of engine, and the difference lies in what each platform lays around that engine.

The figure draws the layers. Node adds the ability to read files, listen on a network port and see its own environment, and that is why it is where servers, tools and build scripts are written. This lesson covers what that platform provides, the two ways that Node loads modules, and how configuration reaches a program.

diagram.alt: A stack of layers. Your JavaScript sits on top, then a layer of platform APIs, then the engine and event loop, then the operating system. The platform layer is Node's file, network and process APIs in one view and the browser's page APIs in the other.
diagram.caption: The same language on two platforms. Use the buttons to swap the platform layer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what Node adds to JavaScript, choose between ES modules and CommonJS, and read environment variables safely as strings.
intro.whyItMatters: Every Node program starts by loading modules and reading configuration, so the details here come up in nearly every file you write.

recap.keyIdea: Node is the V8 engine with a platform of files, network and processes, and the module system and environment variables are the two parts of it that every program meets first.

blocks.text: Node pairs the V8 engine with an event loop and APIs for files, networks and processes, and it has no window or document. It loads code as ES modules, with import and import.meta.dirname, or as CommonJS, with require and __dirname, and the file extension or the package.json type field decides which.

Built-in modules carry the node: prefix, and environment variables arrive as strings or undefined, so a program parses them and supplies a default, taking care over the difference between a missing value and an empty one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks inside the event loop that Node adds, and shows in what order callbacks run and what blocks them.

lessons.title: The Node event loop

steps.headline: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so callbacks take turns, and the waiting for files and networks happens outside it.

lead.text: It is easy to take async to mean that several things run at once, and in Node that is not true of your code. All the JavaScript runs on a single thread, one callback at a time, and a callback runs to its end before the next begins. What goes on in parallel is the waiting: when you ask for a file, the work of reading it is done by libuv and the operating system, off the thread, and when the data is ready the callback joins a queue and waits its turn.

The mechanism that picks the next callback from the queues is the **event loop**, and the figure shows its shape. It is the reason a Node server can have thousands of connections open at once while using one thread, because most of the time each of them is waiting, and a callback is needed only when something arrives.

afterFigure.text: The same arrangement explains the weakness. A callback that does not finish holds up every callback queued behind it, and the last half of this lesson is about that.

lead.text: The script below schedules a timer, a nextTick callback and a promise callback before it logs sync. Decide where the promise callback's line appears among the four, before the next screen gives the queues.

reveal.text: The next screen names the queues and gives their order, and shows how an ES module differs.

steps.headline: After the running code finishes, the nextTick queue runs first, then the promise queue, and both run before the loop moves on.

lead.text: Between the main script and the timers there are two queues that are emptied first. The **nextTick queue** holds callbacks given to process.nextTick, and it runs as soon as the current operation completes. Next the **promise queue**, which holds the callbacks of .then and the code after an await, runs until it is empty. Only then does the event loop go on to its next phase. In a CommonJS file this gives sync, tick, promise, and then the timeout.

The order of the two queues has one exception, which the second view shows. An ES module is itself evaluated inside a promise job, so when the main script of an ES module finishes, the promise queue is already running and its callbacks go first: the output is sync, promise, tick. Code that depends on the difference is fragile, and a safe habit is to use promises, and to keep nextTick for the few places in Node's own style that need it.

afterFigure.text: Because both queues run before any timer, a promise callback that keeps scheduling another can starve the loop, much as a spinning loop would.

reveal.text: Writing the lines in the order the code runs them is the way to check this, queue by queue.

steps.headline: Inside an I/O callback setImmediate always runs before a zero-delay timer, but from the main script the order is not fixed.

lead.text: The event loop goes round a ring of phases, shown in the figure. The timers phase runs the callbacks of setTimeout whose time has come, the poll phase handles I/O callbacks, and the check phase runs the callbacks of setImmediate. After the check phase come the close events, and then the loop starts another turn.

That ring decides the order of two calls that look alike. If you call setTimeout(f, 0) and setImmediate(g) from inside an I/O callback, the loop is in the poll phase and the check phase comes next, so g always runs before f. From the main script, nothing fixes it: it depends on whether the loop reached the timers phase before one millisecond had passed, and a run on a busy machine may differ from another. A test should not depend on the order of the two there.

afterFigure.text: The timer's delay is also a minimum and not a promise: the callback runs when the loop gets to it after the time has passed, which may be later.

diagram.alt: The phases of one turn of the event loop in order: timers, poll for I/O callbacks, check for setImmediate, and close events, then back to timers. One view marks the loop at the start of a turn, and the other marks it inside an I/O callback.

reveal.text: From the main script the answer would be less certain, because the loop would be at the start of a turn.

steps.headline: Trace the four-line script from the start of the lesson through the queues.

workedSteps.text: All the synchronous code runs first. The script registers a timer, a nextTick callback and a promise callback, then logs sync.
The script has finished, so Node empties the nextTick queue before anything else.
Next it empties the promise queue.
Only then does the loop reach the timers phase and run the timer callback. Count the callbacks that were waiting when the script finished.

steps.headline: A long synchronous task holds up every other callback, because there is only one thread to run them on.

lead.text: Since callbacks take turns, one that takes a long time delays all the others, including timers, incoming requests and promise callbacks. The figure shows a timer set for 10 milliseconds and then a synchronous loop that spins for a full second. The timer is due after 10 milliseconds, but the loop is holding the thread, so the callback runs only when it ends, after about 1000 milliseconds. The delay is a minimum, and here it has been exceeded by a long way.

This is what goes wrong when a server does heavy computation in a request handler. While one request is being processed, no other request is served, and a thread that is busy for 200 milliseconds on each of ten requests that arrive together delays the tenth by 2000 milliseconds. Writing await in front of a CPU-bound function does not help, because await waits for a promise and the loop still runs on the same thread.

diagram.alt: A time axis from 0 to 1000 milliseconds. In one view the main thread is occupied by a spinning loop for the whole time, and a timer due at 10 ms fires only at the end. In the other the heavy work runs in a worker thread and the timer fires at about 10 ms.
diagram.caption: A busy thread delays everything queued behind it. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Work out how late a short timer runs when a long synchronous loop starts right after it is set.

reveal.text: The timer does not fire early to make up the time, so the delay is the whole length of the loop.

steps.headline: CPU-heavy work belongs in a worker thread or another process, so that the main thread stays free for callbacks.

lead.text: Work that waits, such as reading a file or calling another server, is already handled well, because libuv and the operating system do the waiting. Work that computes, such as hashing a large file, compressing an image or parsing a huge document, is different, because the computation itself needs a thread and the main one is shared with every other request.

Node provides two ways to give it another. The node:worker_threads module runs a JavaScript file on a separate thread, and the two communicate by messages, so the main thread stays free, as the second view of the earlier figure showed. A separate process, started with node:child_process, does the same with more isolation. For modest work it is often enough to split it into small pieces and yield between them.

afterFigure.text: Choosing between them comes down to the size of the job: a few milliseconds can stay where it is, and anything that is noticeable to a user belongs elsewhere.

lead.text: Take the remedy from the last screen and name the built-in module that supplies it, for a handler that must hash a large file without stalling other requests.

reveal.text: For work that is already asynchronous, such as reading the file, no such move is needed.

lessons.orientation: Predict the order of synchronous code, process.nextTick, promises, timers and setImmediate, and explain why blocking the loop stalls everything.
lessons.nextAction: Say how text becomes bytes in a Buffer and how a stream moves a large file in chunks.

blocks.text: Write five lines in a Node script that log sync, a nextTick callback, a promise callback, a zero-delay timer and a setImmediate callback, and the output will not follow the order of the code. In the main script of a CommonJS file the line for sync comes first, then tick, then promise, and the timer after them, while the same calls made inside a file-read callback put the immediate callback before the timer. The two lists in the figure are what Node printed on one machine.

The order is not arbitrary, and the rules for it come from how Node runs everything on one thread. Learning them tells you which code can safely wait for another, why a timer can run late, and what it costs to leave a long computation in a request handler.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict the order of synchronous code, nextTick, promise, timer and setImmediate callbacks, and say why a long synchronous task stalls everything.
intro.whyItMatters: A server that mishandles the loop works in testing and freezes under load.

recap.keyIdea: Node runs JavaScript on one thread in a fixed order of queues and phases, so a long synchronous task delays everything queued behind it.

blocks.text: After the synchronous code, Node empties the nextTick queue and then the promise queue, and only then goes round the phases of the event loop, where an I/O callback is followed by setImmediate before any timer. From the main script the order of a zero-delay timer and setImmediate is not fixed.

Everything runs on one thread, so a long loop makes a timer late and a server's other requests wait. Waiting for I/O is already off the thread, and CPU-heavy work belongs in a worker thread or another process.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the data that moves through that loop, as bytes in buffers and as streams that process a file in pieces.

lessons.title: Files, streams and buffers

lead.text: A string has five characters, one of which is an accented letter. Decide how many bytes it takes when it is written to a file as UTF-8, before the next screen explains what a byte count is.

reveal.text: The next screen explains how text becomes bytes, and why the count and the length can differ.

steps.headline: Text is turned into bytes by an encoding, and under UTF-8 a character takes between one and four bytes, so a string's length is not its size.

lead.text: A file, a network connection and a Node **Buffer** hold bytes, which are numbers from 0 to 255, and not characters. A Buffer is a fixed-size block of bytes, and text becomes bytes through an **encoding**. The usual one is **UTF-8**, which gives each ASCII character a single byte and each other character two, three or four: the é in café takes two bytes, the euro sign takes three, and an emoji such as U+1F600 takes four.

JavaScript strings count differently. The length property of a string counts UTF-16 code units, so 'héllo'.length is 5, and the emoji, which needs two code units, has a length of 2. The size in bytes comes from Buffer.byteLength, which for 'héllo' is 6. The two numbers agree only for plain ASCII text, and a program that uses length to size a buffer or to check a limit on bytes is wrong for any other.

afterFigure.text: A character that is outside the first 128 is the first to expose such a bug, and so tests for a size limit should include one.

diagram.alt: A table of four strings with their length and their size in UTF-8 bytes. Hello has length 5 and 5 bytes. Hello with an accented e has length 5 and 6 bytes. The euro sign has length 1 and 3 bytes. The emoji U+1F600 has length 2 and 4 bytes.

steps.headline: A Buffer can be written as text, as hex or as base64, and each is a different way of showing the same bytes.

lead.text: Bytes are rarely shown as they are, so there are standard ways to write them as text. **Hex** writes each byte as two hexadecimal digits, so the two bytes of 'hi', 68 and 69, become the string "6869", which is a form that suits checksums and logs. **Base64** packs the bytes three at a time into four characters from a set of 64 letters, digits and symbols, with = padding at the end, and the same two bytes become "aGk=". It is made for sending bytes through channels that carry only text, such as JSON.

In Node the conversions are Buffer.from("hi").toString("hex") and Buffer.from("hi").toString("base64"), and the reverse is Buffer.from("aGk=", "base64").toString(), which gives back "hi". Nothing in a string says which encoding produced it, so a program has to know.

afterFigure.text: Base64 is not encryption. Anyone can reverse it, and its output is about a third longer than its input.

steps.headline: A stream moves data in chunks, so a program can process a file of any size while holding only one chunk in memory.

lead.text: The function fs.readFile returns the contents of a file only when all of it has been read, so the whole file is in memory at once. For a 4 GB file that is more than many machines can spare, and the program fails. A **stream** avoids this by delivering the data in pieces. fs.createReadStream gives chunks of 64 KiB, that is 65536 bytes, one after another, and the program handles each as it arrives and releases it.

There are four kinds of stream: Readable ones produce data, Writable ones consume it, Duplex ones do both and Transform ones change what passes through. Chaining a Readable through a Transform into a Writable is a pipeline, and it is how Node programs copy, compress and convert files whose size nobody knows in advance.

afterFigure.text: A stream also begins work sooner. The first chunk can be processed while the rest of the file is still being read.

lead.text: The writable stream below holds at most ten bytes comfortably and drains slowly. Decide how many of three writes return false, before the next screen explains the signal.

reveal.text: The next screen explains what false means and what the producer is supposed to do next.

steps.headline: write() returns false when the waiting data reaches the high-water mark, and the producer should pause until the stream emits drain.

lead.text: A stream has a limit on the bytes it will hold in its internal buffer, called the **highWaterMark**, which is 65536 bytes by default for byte streams. A producer that is faster than its consumer, such as a program that reads a file quickly and writes to a slow network connection, would otherwise pile up data in that buffer without limit. The stream therefore tells the producer when it has reached the limit, by returning **false** from write(). That signal is called **backpressure**.

The write is still accepted, as the third view of the figure shows. False is a request and not a refusal: the producer should stop writing and wait for the drain event, which the stream emits when its buffer has emptied. A producer that ignores the signal works on small tests and uses more and more memory under real load.

afterFigure.text: Writing this by hand is easy to get wrong, which is why pipeline from node:stream/promises is the usual way to connect streams: it pauses and resumes the producer, and it closes every stream if one of them fails.

diagram.alt: A horizontal gauge of the bytes waiting inside a writable stream, with a marked line at the high-water mark of 10 bytes. After a 5-byte write the gauge holds 5 and write returns true. blocks.text: The word café has four characters, and written to a file it takes five bytes, because the é is stored as two. In Node the first number is the string's length and the second is what Buffer.byteLength reports, and a program that treats one as the other goes wrong as soon as someone types an accent. Text is bytes only through an encoding, and the encoding decides how many.

Bytes then have to travel: from a disk, through a network, into a program that might be given a file of several gigabytes. This lesson follows them. It begins with the buffer that holds bytes and the ways of writing them as hex and base64, and goes on to streams, which carry data in pieces, and to the one signal that keeps a fast producer from drowning a slow consumer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the bytes of a string in UTF-8, convert between hex, base64 and text, and say when a stream's write signals backpressure.
intro.whyItMatters: Sizes, limits and large files are where text handling and memory use go wrong in real services.

recap.keyIdea: Text becomes bytes through an encoding whose size differs from the string's length, and streams carry those bytes in chunks while backpressure keeps a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer.

blocks.text: A Buffer holds bytes, and UTF-8 turns a character into one to four of them, so Buffer.byteLength can be larger than a string's length. The same bytes can be written as hex or base64, and 'hi' becomes 6869 or aGk=.

A stream moves a file in chunks, so memory use depends on the chunk and not on the file, and write() returns false once the waiting bytes reach the highWaterMark. The producer then waits for drain, which pipeline does for you.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these streams to serve HTTP, where a request arrives as a stream of bytes and a response must be written correctly.

lessons.title: Serving HTTP

steps.headline: An HTTP handler is a function that receives a request and builds a response, and everything that crosses the connection is text and bytes.

lead.text: A web server does one job over and over: it reads a request and writes a response. The figure shows the text of each. The first line of a request carries a **method**, which says what is wanted, and a URL, which says where, and the lines after it are **headers**, such as the one that says which formats the client accepts. A request may also carry a body. The response begins with a **status** line, which says what happened, then headers, then a body.

In Node's http module, a handler is a function (req, res) => { ... } that is called for every request. The object req gives the method in req.method, the URL in req.url, the headers in req.headers, and the body as a stream of bytes, as in the last lesson. The object res is where the response is built: res.statusCode and res.setHeader set the status and the headers, and res.end(body) sends the body and completes it.

afterFigure.text: A handler is ordinary JavaScript running on the event loop, so everything said there applies. A handler that blocks for a second blocks every other request.

lead.text: A handler splits req.url on slashes to find an id. Decide how long the piece that should hold the id is when the URL has a query string, before the next screen shows the safe way.

reveal.text: The next screen shows how to parse the URL, so that the query string stays out of the way.

steps.headline: A router chooses a handler from the method and the pathname, and the pathname must be parsed from req.url, because that includes the query string.

lead.text: The value of req.url is everything after the host, so for a request to /users/42?x=1 it holds the query string as well. Comparing it with /users/42 fails for that request, and splitting it leaves "42?x=1" as the last piece. The safe course is to parse it with the URL class: new URL(req.url, "http://localhost") gives an object whose pathname is /users/42 and whose searchParams.get("x") is "1", and splitting the pathname on slashes gives ["", "users", "42"], where the id is at index 2.

A **router** is the code that picks a handler. It looks at the method and the pathname together: GET on /users/42 goes to a handler that reads a user, POST on /users goes to one that creates a user, and a method that the path does not allow gets a 405 response. The base in the URL call is arbitrary, since only the path matters, and it is needed because req.url has no host.

afterFigure.text: A router checked by method first is easy to extend, because adding a route adds one row and leaves the others alone.

diagram.alt: A router choosing a handler from the method and the path. GET on /users/42 reaches getUser. POST on /users reaches createUser. DELETE on /users/42 matches the path but not the method, so the answer is 405.
diagram.caption: The router reads the method and the pathname together. Use the buttons to try three requests.

reveal.text: The id is still text, "42", and a handler converts it with Number before using it as a number.

steps.headline: The status code tells the client what happened, so it has to match the outcome, and the default of 200 makes a failure look like success.

lead.text: Every response has a **status code**, a three-digit number in which the first digit gives the class. A 2xx code means success, a 4xx code means that the request was at fault, and a 5xx code means that the server was. The codes a handler uses most are 200 for a normal answer, 201 for something created, with a Location header naming it, 400 for a malformed request, 404 for a resource that does not exist, 405 for a method the path does not allow, with an Allow header listing the ones it does, and 500 for a fault in the server.

Node's default is res.statusCode = 200. A handler that finds no user and writes "not found" in the body, without setting a status, tells the client that the request succeeded. Clients, caches and monitors read the status and not the body, so the status has to say it.

afterFigure.text: Choosing 400 or 404 is a matter of who made the mistake. Bad JSON in a request is the client's, and so is a request for an id that does not exist.

diagram.alt: Two tables of status codes. Success: 200 for a normal answer and 201 for something created. Failure: 400 for a malformed request, 401 for missing credentials, 404 for a missing resource, 405 for a wrong method and 500 for a fault in the server.
diagram.caption: A status says what happened, so it must match. Use the buttons to switch between success and failure.

lead.text: Decide who is at fault when a client sends a body that is not valid JSON, and choose the status that says so.

reveal.text: A 500 here would tell monitoring that the server is broken, when in fact it is working as intended.

steps.headline: Choose the status for four requests to a user service that has routes for GET and POST only.

workedSteps.text: A GET for /users/42 finds the user and sends it back.
A POST to /users with a valid body creates a user, which has not existed before.
A GET for /users/999 finds no such user.
A DELETE for /users/42 reaches a path that exists, but the method is not one the service allows.
Enter the status for the last request.

steps.headline: A handler must set a status and a content type and call res.end(), because returning from the function does not finish the response.

lead.text: A response is a promise to the client that the handler keeps in three parts. The status is 200 unless it is set. The Content-Type header says what the body is, and for JSON it should be application/json, with the body produced by JSON.stringify, because a client reads the header to decide how to parse. And res.end() must be called, because it is the call that marks the response as complete.

The third part is the one that is forgotten. A handler that calls res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/plain" }) and res.write("ok") and then returns has sent a status and some text, but the response is still open. Node does not end it, and no error is raised, so the client sits and waits. It receives the headers and the text, and then nothing, until it or a proxy in between gives up.

afterFigure.text: In an async handler the same slip is easy to make with an early return in one branch, which is why the end of every branch is worth checking.

diagram.alt: A request goes into a handler and a response comes out. In the first view the handler ends the response and the client has the answer. In the second the handler never ends the response and the client keeps waiting.
diagram.caption: The response is finished only by res.end(). Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Read a handler that sends a status, a header and some text, and decide what the client sees when the function returns without ending the response.

reveal.text: Writing the body in a single res.end call is the simplest way to keep the contract.

steps.headline: A request body arrives as chunks of bytes, which the handler joins, decodes and parses, and invalid JSON is answered with 400.

lead.text: The body of a request is a stream, as in the last lesson, so it comes in pieces that can split anywhere, even in the middle of a word, as the figure shows. A handler collects the chunks as they arrive, joins them when the stream ends, decodes the bytes to text, and then parses the text. Reading the first chunk and parsing it would work for small bodies on a fast connection, and fail for others.

The last step can fail. JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError when the text is not valid JSON, so the handler wraps it in try and catch and answers 400 when it throws. Letting the error escape would make the server answer 500, or crash, and either one blames the server for what the client sent.

afterFigure.text: After parsing, the value is still unknown to the type system, as the earlier lesson on types at the edges explained, and has to be checked before the program relies on its shape.

diagram.alt: Three stages of reading a JSON request body. The body arrives in chunks that can split anywhere. The chunks are joined and decoded to text. The text is parsed, which gives an object or throws a syntax error that the handler answers with 400.

lead.text: Follow a handler that reports a missing user only in the body text, and decide what a client that reads the status would conclude.

reveal.text: Monitors, caches and client libraries read the status code and not the body, so this response would be counted as a success everywhere.

lessons.orientation: Read a Node HTTP handler and predict the status, headers and body it sends, including routing from req.url and what happens when a response is never ended.
lessons.nextAction: Predict how Promise.all and Promise.allSettled behave when some tasks fail, and why a loop of awaits runs one task at a time.

blocks.text: A web server reads a few lines of text and answers with a few lines more. The request in the figure is a method and a URL followed by headers, and the response is a status line, headers and a body, and the whole of an HTTP service in Node is a function that turns one into the other. Most of the bugs in such a function come from details around the edges: a URL that carries a query string, a status that was never set, a response that was never finished.

This lesson reads handlers closely, and says for each what the client will receive. It covers routing from the method and the path, the status codes that handlers return, the contract that every response must keep, and the way a request body is read and parsed.

diagram.alt: The text of an HTTP request and the text of its response. The request line has a method and a URL, followed by headers. The response has a status line, headers and a body.
diagram.caption: What travels over the connection. Use the buttons to see the request and the response.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a Node HTTP handler and predict its status, headers and body, including routing from req.url and what happens when a response is never ended.
intro.whyItMatters: The same handler shape is the base of every Node web framework, so reading one carefully is reading all of them.

recap.keyIdea: A handler turns a request into a response, so routing must parse the URL, the status must say what happened, and the response is complete only after res.end().

blocks.text: A handler receives the method, the URL, the headers and a body stream, and builds a status, headers and a body. req.url includes the query string, so the pathname is read through the URL class, and the router picks a handler from the method and the pathname together.

The status defaults to 200, so failures need their own: 400 for a malformed body, 404 for a missing resource, 405 for a wrong method and 201 for a creation. A response is finished only by res.end(), and a request body is joined from its chunks and parsed, with an invalid body answered by 400.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to errors and concurrency, which covers how promises fail and how to run several tasks at once in Node.

lessons.title: Errors and concurrency

lead.text: Three promises are passed to one combinator, and the second of them rejects with an error whose message is boom. Decide what the catch block receives, before the next screen describes the four combinators.

reveal.text: The next screen describes the four combinators and what each does with a rejection.

steps.headline: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection, allSettled reports every outcome, race settles with the first to settle, and any fulfils with the first to fulfil.

lead.text: When several promises are in flight, a **combinator** turns them into one. Promise.all waits for all of them to fulfil and gives an array of their values in order, but as soon as any one rejects, it rejects with that error and the results of the others are lost. Promise.allSettled never rejects: it waits until every promise has settled and gives an array of objects, each with a status of "fulfilled" or "rejected", and a value or a reason.

The other two answer a different question, which is who is first. Promise.race settles with the first promise to settle, whether it fulfils or rejects, which suits a timeout. Promise.any settles with the first to *fulfil* and ignores rejections until all of them have rejected, when it throws an AggregateError. The choice among the four depends on what a failure should mean for the whole group.

afterFigure.text: Promise.all does not cancel the tasks that are left. They go on running, and only their results are discarded.

diagram.alt: A table of four promise combinators and what each does when the inputs settle. all waits for every fulfilment and rejects on the first rejection. allSettled waits for every outcome. race settles with the first outcome. any fulfils with the first fulfilment.
diagram.caption: Four combinators and the moment each one settles. Use the buttons to see what each waits for.

lead.text: Use the combinator that never rejects on four tasks of which two fail, and count the entries that report a failure.

reveal.text: Promise.all on the same four would have rejected with the first error, and the two fulfilments would have been lost.

steps.headline: await in a loop runs tasks one after another, while Promise.all over promises that have already started runs them together.

lead.text: An await pauses the function until its promise settles. Written inside a for loop, it therefore starts the second task only after the first has finished, and three independent tasks of 50 milliseconds take about 150 milliseconds. Starting all three first, for example with tasks.map(run), and awaiting them together with Promise.all, lets the waiting overlap, so the total is the longest single task, about 50 milliseconds.

The figure shows both. Overlap is safe only when the tasks do not depend on each other, and if they do, the loop is correct. The third view shows what a failure does: the call rejects as soon as one task rejects, here at 30 ms, and the slower task, which nobody can cancel, runs on to its end.

afterFigure.text: The speed-up comes from the waiting overlapping, as in the event loop lesson. It does not make the JavaScript itself run in parallel.

diagram.alt: A time axis from 0 to 150 milliseconds. Awaited one after another, three 50 ms tasks follow each other and take 150 ms. Started together, they overlap and take 50 ms. If one rejects under Promise.all, the whole call rejects at once while the slower task keeps running.
diagram.caption: Three 50 ms tasks scheduled three ways. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Add up the time for three independent tasks that are awaited one after another, using the first view of the figure.

reveal.text: Starting them together would reduce this to the longest task alone.

steps.headline: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, and a missing await lets a rejection escape the try block around it.

lead.text: The method forEach calls its callback for each element and does not look at what the callback returns. When the callback is an async function, it returns a promise, and forEach discards it. The loop therefore finishes at once, and the code after it runs before any of the awaits inside the callbacks have completed, as the figure shows: the length of the list is still 0. The same applies to other methods that take callbacks and expect plain values.

The remedy is to keep the promises. await Promise.all(items.map(async x => ...)) collects them and waits, and a for ... of loop with await inside is the form to use when the work must happen in order. A related mistake is calling an async function inside try without awaiting it. The function returns a rejected promise, the catch block never sees it, because no error was thrown in the block, and the rejection escapes.

afterFigure.text: In both cases the code reads as though it waits, and the only sign that it does not is a result that is missing when you look for it.

diagram.alt: Two loops over 1, 2 and 3 that push each number to a list after an await, followed by a log of the list's length. With forEach the log shows 0, because forEach does not wait. With a for loop and await it shows 3.

reveal.text: Awaiting a promise lets other code run in the meantime, which here includes the line after the forEach.

steps.headline: Rewrite the forEach so that the list is full when the next line runs.

workedSteps.text: The problem is that forEach discards the promises, so nothing waits for the pushes.
The first change is to use map, which returns an array of the promises that the callback returned.
workedSteps.math: const ps = [1, 2, 3].map(async n => { await null; out.push(n); });

workedSteps.text: The second change is to wait for all of them with Promise.all, before the log runs.
With the pushes finished, count what the list holds when the log runs.

steps.headline: A rejection that nobody handles ends the Node process with a non-zero exit code, and a handler for it only hides the failure unless it logs.

lead.text: A promise that rejects needs a consumer: an await inside a try, a .catch, or a second argument to .then. When none is attached by the time the loop moves on, Node treats the rejection as an uncaught error. Since Node 15 the default is to print the error and end the process with exit code 1, as the first view of the figure shows, which turns a forgotten await into a visible crash instead of a silent failure.

A handler registered with process.on("unhandledRejection", ...) replaces that default. The process then goes on and exits with code 0, so the handler has to log or report the error itself, and a service that adds an empty one has made the failure invisible. The better course is to fix the cause, that is, to handle the promise where it is created.

diagram.alt: A program that rejects a promise nobody handles. By default Node prints the error and exits with code 1. With a handler for unhandledRejection, the program continues and exits with code 0.
diagram.caption: A rejection that nobody handles. Use the buttons to compare the default and a handler.

lead.text: Run a rejected promise through Node with no handler anywhere, and read the exit code a shell would see.

reveal.text: With a handler registered, the same program would exit with 0, which is why handlers should log.

steps.headline: An AbortController lets the caller cancel work, and the cancelled operation rejects with an AbortError.

lead.text: Promises cannot be cancelled once started, so work that may have to stop is given a signal. A caller creates an AbortController, passes its signal to the API, and calls controller.abort() when it wants the work to stop. APIs that accept a signal, such as fetch and the promise form of setTimeout in node:timers/promises, then stop and reject their promise with an error named AbortError.

This is how a timeout is built for a request. A timer calls abort() after the allowed time, the request is cancelled, and the code that awaited it receives an AbortError, which it can tell apart from other failures by its name. Without the signal the request would carry on to its end, and nothing could stop it.

afterFigure.text: A signal does not force anything to stop. It is a request that the operation honours, and operations that do not take a signal cannot be cancelled this way.

lead.text: Cancel a request that was given a signal, and name the error that the awaiting code receives.

reveal.text: A timeout can be built from the same pieces, with a timer that calls abort after the allowed time.

blocks.text: Three tasks are started at once, and the second one fails. What should the program do with the first and third, which succeeded? The answer is not the same for every program, and the four promise combinators exist because it is not: Promise.all gives up on the whole group at the first failure, Promise.allSettled keeps every outcome, and race and any care only about whichever promise gets there first.

Alongside the choice come the mistakes that make asynchronous code fail without a message, such as a loop that awaits nothing, a missing await inside a try block, or a rejection that no one has caught. This lesson sets out what each combinator does, why await in a loop is slow and forEach with async is wrong, what Node does with an unhandled rejection, and how to stop work that is no longer wanted.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict how Promise.all, allSettled, race and forEach with async behave, and what an unhandled rejection does to a Node process.
intro.whyItMatters: Asynchronous mistakes rarely raise an error where they are made, so they are best caught by reading.

recap.keyIdea: Promise combinators decide what one failure means for a group of tasks, await in a loop serialises the work, and a promise nobody awaits or handles fails silently or ends the process.

blocks.text: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection and discards the rest, allSettled reports every outcome, race settles with the first and any with the first fulfilment. Awaiting in a loop makes tasks run one after another, taking the sum of their times, and Promise.all over started promises takes the longest.

forEach ignores the promises of an async callback, so the code after it runs first, and a promise that is neither awaited nor handled is an unhandled rejection, which ends the process with exit code 1. An AbortController signal lets a caller cancel work, which then rejects with an AbortError.

lessons.title: Packages, versions and tests

lead.text: Two version numbers differ only in the minor part, one with a nine and one with a ten. Decide which is the newer, before the next screen gives the rules for reading a version.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the rules, and shows why comparing versions as text goes wrong.

steps.headline: A semantic version has the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and each part says how much changed, so a program can decide which updates are safe.

lead.text: A **semantic version**, or semver, is three whole numbers separated by dots, such as 1.4.2. The **patch** number rises for a bug fix, the **minor** number rises for a new feature that does not break existing use, and the **major** number rises for a change that may break callers of the library. Raising a part sets every part to its right back to 0, so the minor bump of 1.4.2 is 1.5.0, and the major bump is 2.0.0.

The parts are compared as numbers, one at a time from the left, and never as text. As text, "1.10.0" sorts before "1.9.0", because the character 1 comes before 9, but as versions 1.10.0 is the newer, since 10 is greater than 9. A version may also have a suffix after a hyphen, such as 1.2.3-beta.1, which marks a **prerelease** that is older than 1.2.3 itself and is not offered to ranges that do not ask for it.

afterFigure.text: The numbers are a promise by the library's author, and nothing checks it. A major change released as a patch breaks callers all the same.

steps.headline: A range in package.json says which versions are acceptable: ^ allows changes up to the next major version, and ~ allows patch changes only.

lead.text: A dependency is listed in package.json with a **version range**, and the range decides which published versions npm may install. The caret form ^1.2.3 means 1.2.3 or any later version up to, but not including, 2.0.0, so it accepts 1.2.9 and 1.9.0 and rejects 2.0.0. The tilde form ~1.2.3 is narrower, and accepts only patch changes: up to, but not including, 1.3.0. A bare 1.2.3 accepts that version alone.

The caret is stricter below 1.0.0, where a library is not yet stable. It keeps the leftmost part that is not zero fixed, so ^0.2.3 accepts 0.2.9 and rejects 0.3.0, and ^0.0.3 accepts 0.0.3 alone. Prereleases are left out unless the range itself names one, so ^1.2.3 does not accept 1.2.3-beta.1.

afterFigure.text: A range is therefore a statement of trust, in how carefully the author follows semver.

diagram.alt: Three version ranges checked against candidate versions. The caret range 1.2.3 accepts 1.2.9 and 1.9.0 and rejects 1.2.2 and 2.0.0. The tilde range 1.2.3 accepts 1.2.9 and rejects 1.3.0. The caret range 0.2.3 accepts 0.2.9 and rejects 0.3.0 and 1.0.0.
diagram.caption: Which versions each range allows. Use the buttons to compare three ranges.

lead.text: Check five candidate versions against the caret range ^1.2.3, including one that is older, one that is the next major, and a prerelease.

reveal.text: The lower end is part of the range, so 1.2.3 itself would be accepted.

steps.headline: Work out which versions the range ^0.2.3 accepts, one rule at a time.

workedSteps.text: Find the leftmost part that is not zero. The major part is 0, so the first non-zero part is the minor, 2.
The caret keeps that part fixed. So the range starts at the stated version and stops before the next minor.
Check four candidates against it: 0.2.2 is below the lower end, 0.2.3 is the lower end, 0.2.9 is inside, and 0.3.0 is the upper end, which is excluded.
Count how many of the four candidates the range accepts.

steps.headline: package-lock.json records the exact version of every dependency, and npm ci installs exactly that, so every machine gets the same tree.

lead.text: A range leaves room: ^1.2.3 today installs 1.2.3, and next month it may install 1.9.0. That is useful for taking fixes, and awkward for a build that has to be repeated exactly. The file package-lock.json settles it. When npm installs, it writes the exact version it chose for every package, including the dependencies of dependencies, and later installs read the file.

The two commands differ in how they treat it. npm install may choose a newer version that the range allows, and rewrites the lockfile when it does. npm ci installs exactly the versions in the lockfile, and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree, which makes it the command for a build server and for tests. The lockfile belongs in version control. Deleting it to clear an error removes the one thing that makes installs repeatable, and every dependency may then change at once.

afterFigure.text: The range expresses what you are willing to accept, and the lockfile records what you actually got.

diagram.alt: Two install commands for a project whose package.json asks for a library at ^1.2.3 and whose lockfile records 1.2.3. npm install may move the library to 1.9.0 and rewrite the lockfile. npm ci installs exactly 1.2.3 from the lockfile.

steps.headline: node --test runs files that use node:test and node:assert, groups tests with describe and it, and fails with a non-zero exit code when any test fails.

lead.text: Node includes a test runner, so a project can test its code without installing a framework. A test file imports describe and it from node:test, and an assertion library from node:assert. Each it block is one test, and a test passes if it finishes without throwing. The assertions do the throwing: assert.strictEqual(actual, expected) compares with ===, and assert.deepStrictEqual compares the contents of objects and arrays.

The command node --test finds the test files, runs them and prints a report with a count of tests passed and failed. For a failure it shows the expected and the actual values, as the figure's report does. The command ends with exit code 1 if any test failed, and that code is what a continuous integration job reads in order to stop.

afterFigure.text: A deliberately failing test, written first and then made to pass, is the surest way to know that the test can fail at all.

diagram.alt: A test file with three tests for an add function, and its report. Two pass and one fails, because add of 2 and 2 is 4 and the test expected 5. The report shows the expected and actual values, and the exit code is 1.

lessons.orientation: Read a semver range and say which versions it accepts, explain what a lockfile fixes, and read a node:test file.
lessons.nextAction: Design a small typed service that validates its configuration and its input, and shuts down cleanly.

blocks.text: A library you depend on releases version 1.4.2 on Monday and 1.5.0 on Friday, and your package.json says ^1.4.2. Whether Friday's version arrives on your machine depends on two small pieces of notation, the range and the lockfile, and on a promise from the library's author about what the middle number means. A program that installs the wrong version fails in a way that its source code does not explain.
This lesson covers how versions are written and compared, which versions a range accepts, how the lockfile fixes the result and how a test file is read.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a semver range and say which versions it accepts, explain what a lockfile fixes, and read a node:test file.
intro.whyItMatters: Installing the wrong version, or a different one on each machine, is a common cause of failures that cannot be reproduced.

recap.keyIdea: A version range says which updates are acceptable, the lockfile records the exact versions chosen, and a test file turns the checking of both into something a machine can run.

blocks.text: A version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, compared as numbers, so 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0. The range ^1.2.3 accepts up to but not including 2.0.0, ~1.2.3 accepts patch changes only, and the caret is stricter below 1.0.0, where ^0.2.3 stops before 0.3.0.

package-lock.json records the exact versions installed, and npm ci installs exactly those. A node:test file groups tests with describe and it, uses assertions that throw on failure, and node --test exits with code 1 if any test fails.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson puts the course together in a small typed service that reads its configuration at startup and checks everything that enters it.

lessons.title: A typed service

lead.text: A start-up check collects every problem before it throws. Decide how many problems it reports for a configuration with a bad port and a missing database URL.

reveal.text: The next screen explains why a service reads its configuration once, at startup, and reports everything wrong at once.

steps.headline: A service reads and validates its configuration once, at startup, so that a mistake stops it at once, with every problem listed.

lead.text: Configuration is the first place where outside data meets the program, and the rule from the earlier lessons applies to it unchanged: environment variables are strings or undefined, and nothing says they are right. A service that reads process.env.PORT in the middle of a request finds out about a missing or misspelt variable on the first request that needs it, perhaps hours after it started. A service that reads all of its configuration once, in one module, and checks it there, finds out before it has served anything.

The loader below converts and checks each value, and collects the problems in a list instead of throwing at the first. It reads the port with Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000) and tests it with Number.isInteger, and it requires the database URL. If the list is not empty it throws a single error that names every problem, so the person starting the service fixes them all in one go. If it is empty, it returns an object with real types, a number for the port, and the rest of the program never touches process.env again.

afterFigure.text: Failing at once is called failing fast, and it moves the discovery of a mistake from the busiest moment to the quietest one.

diagram.alt: Reading configuration at startup. With PORT set to abc and DATABASE_URL missing, the loader throws once with both problems listed. With valid values it returns a typed object.
diagram.caption: Configuration checked once, before the service starts. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Convert a port that has a stray letter on the end, using the conversion the loader applies to every numeric setting.

reveal.text: parseInt would give 80 here, which is why the whole-string check with Number is the safer choice for configuration.

steps.headline: Validation belongs at the boundary, where a parser turns unknown input into a typed value once, and a cast checks nothing.

lead.text: A request body is outside data too. The tempting way to type it is a cast, JSON.parse(text) as CreateUser, and the figure shows what it does: the code compiles, the body goes on to the database with its age as a string, and the error appears there, or worse, not at all. The cast cannot help, because it is erased, as you saw in the lesson on types at the edges.

The alternative is a **parser**: a function that takes unknown and returns either a typed value or a reason for refusing it. It checks each field with a real test at run time, such as typeof input.age === "number", and it does so in one place, before any handler runs. Every handler after it receives data that has been through the test, so none of them needs to check again, and none of them can forget to. Validating inside each handler leaves a gap in every handler that does not.

afterFigure.text: The idea is to parse, and not merely to check: the output of the parser is a new value with a better type than its input.

diagram.alt: Two ways to turn a request body into a typed value. A cast to CreateUser compiles and checks nothing at run time, so a body with age as a string reaches the database. A parser checks each field and returns an error for the same body.

steps.headline: A Result type is a discriminated union of success and failure, so the compiler makes every caller deal with a failed parse.

lead.text: The parser needs a return type that cannot be ignored. Returning CreateUser | null allows a caller to forget the null, and throwing leaves the failure out of the signature entirely. A discriminated union makes the failure a value that the type system can see: type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string }. The property ok is the discriminant from the lesson on unions.

A handler has to narrow before it can read the value. In if (!r.ok) return 400, the checker removes the failure member for the rest of the function, and after that line r.value is a typed CreateUser. Reading r.value without the check is the compile error in the figure, TS2339, because the failure member has no value. The caller is therefore forced to say what happens when the input is bad.

afterFigure.text: The union can hold more than a message. A list of field errors is often returned, so that a client can show each one.

diagram.alt: A Result type that is either ok with a value or not ok with an error. Reading the value without checking ok first is a compile error. After an ok check the value can be used.
diagram.caption: The type forces the caller to deal with failure. Use the buttons to compare the two uses.

lead.text: A request is partway through when the process is told to stop, and the handler for the signal calls server.close(). Decide when the response arrives, before the next screen gives the full sequence.

steps.headline: On SIGTERM a service stops accepting connections, finishes the requests in flight, closes its resources and then exits with code 0.

lead.text: A platform stops a service by sending it a signal, usually **SIGTERM**, and then waiting. A service that does nothing is killed after a few seconds, and any request in progress is cut off. A service that calls process.exit() in its handler is no better, since it ends at once and drops the same requests. The signal is a chance to finish properly, in a fixed order.

First the server stops accepting new connections, with server.close(), which lets the connections that are already open complete. Second the service waits until the requests in flight have finished, which close() reports through its callback. Third it closes the resources that those requests used, such as the database pool, which cannot be closed earlier without breaking them. Finally it exits with code 0, which tells the platform that the stop was clean. Each step depends on the one before it, and the figure moves through them.

afterFigure.text: Many services also set a deadline, so that a request that never finishes cannot hold up the shutdown for ever, and exit with a non-zero code if it passes.

diagram.alt: Four shutdown steps in order after SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, wait for requests in flight, close the database pool, exit with code 0. Each view highlights one step.
diagram.caption: The order matters, because each step depends on the one before it. Use the buttons to move through the steps.

lead.text: Put the closing of the database pool in its place among four shutdown steps, using the rule that a resource is closed only when nothing is left to use it.

reveal.text: The order is the same for any resource: stop the producers, drain the work, release the resources, exit.

steps.headline: Structured logs with a request id and a health endpoint let an operator see what a service is doing and whether it is well.

lead.text: A service that has been deployed can only be understood through what it reports. A **structured log** writes each event as one line of JSON, such as {"level":"info","requestId":"a1","path":"/users","status":201,"ms":12}, so that a tool can filter and count them. Giving each request an id and putting it in every line it produces lets you follow one request through the router, the parser and the database, even when thousands are interleaved.

A **health endpoint** is a route, often /health, that answers 200 while the service is able to work, and a platform asks it before sending traffic and again at intervals. During graceful shutdown it is the endpoint that starts answering with an error first, so that the platform stops sending requests before the server stops listening. Tests complete the picture: a node:test file that feeds the parser good and bad input and checks the results is how you know the boundary still works after the next change.

afterFigure.text: Logs and health checks cost little to add at the start of a service and a good deal to add during an incident.

lessons.orientation: Design a small HTTP service that parses its configuration and every request body into typed values, fails fast on bad input and shuts down cleanly.
lessons.nextAction: Read and write a small typed Node service: validate its configuration and input at the boundary, return typed results, and shut it down cleanly.

blocks.text: A user service is in production, and a request arrives with the body {"name":"Ada","age":"x"}. The code that handles it is typed, and the compiler checked all of it, but nothing at run time asked whether age was really a number. Whether the service rejects the request, stores a nonsense value, or fails somewhere deeper depends on where, if anywhere, someone decided to look.

This final lesson builds the arrangement that makes the answer certain, from the pieces of the earlier ones. Configuration is read and checked once at startup, every request body is turned into a typed value at the boundary or refused, the code that follows can rely on its types, and the service stops without dropping the work it has started.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to design a small HTTP service that validates its configuration and its input, returns typed results, and shuts down without dropping requests.
intro.whyItMatters: This is where the course's separate lessons become one program, and it is the shape most real Node services have.

recap.keyIdea: A typed service checks data once at each edge, startup configuration and request bodies, so everything inside can trust its types, and it stops by finishing what it started.

blocks.text: The service reads its configuration once at startup and fails fast with every problem listed, and a parser turns each unknown request body into a Result, a discriminated union that forces the handler to deal with failure. A cast would check nothing, so validation sits at the boundary and runs once before any handler.

On SIGTERM it stops accepting connections, waits for requests in flight, closes the database pool and exits with code 0, and structured logs with a request id and a health endpoint show an operator how it is doing. Tests with good and bad input keep the boundary honest.
