questions.onCorrect: With the option on, any index read may miss, so undefined is added to the element type.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the type without the option. With it on, an index read may find nothing, and the type says so.

questions.prompt:
const cfg = { port: 3000, host: "x" } satisfies { port: number | string; host: string };
What is the type of cfg.port?
hints: satisfies checks the object without changing its type.
What type does 3000 have in an object literal?
questions.onCorrect: satisfies leaves the inferred type in place, so port stays number.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the type with an annotation. satisfies keeps the type the value already had.

questions.prompt: Why check the shape with tests, instead of writing input as { port: number }?
hints: Which of the two can be wrong at run time?
questions.onCorrect: A test inspects the actual value, so a payload that fails it is stopped, and the assertion cannot do that.

choices.label: The tests run at run time and make the belief true, while the assertion adds no check.
The assertion would convert the port to a number and hide errors.
The compiler rejects every assertion from unknown.
Tests are faster than assertions at run time.

acceptedIdeas: The tests run at run time and make the belief true, while the assertion adds no check.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tests run at run time and make the belief true, while the assertion adds no check.

misconceptions.feedback: An assertion never converts a value. It only changes what the checker believes.
An assertion from unknown is accepted by the compiler, which is why it is dangerous.
The reason is correctness. An assertion costs nothing at run time, and has nothing to do with speed.

questions.prompt: How many conditions does the complete test contain?
hints: Count the typeof tests and the other tests.
The test joins its conditions with &&.
Add them up.
questions.onCorrect: Each condition excludes one way the data could fail to fit, so all four are needed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four are: typeof input is object, input is not null, the port property is present, and the port is a number.

misconceptions.feedback: The list has two more tests after the first pair: the property and its type.
null needs its own test, because typeof null is also object.

hints: The assertion changes only the checker's belief.
What is the value of cfg.port at run time?
What does + do with a string and a number?
questions.onCorrect: With a string on one side, + joins instead of adding, so the program prints 801.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The port in the text is the string "80", and the assertion does not convert it, so + joins the string with 1 and prints "801".

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the sum of two numbers. The value is still a string, and + joins strings.
The expression adds 1 to the port in some way, so the result differs from the value itself.

questions.prompt:
const input: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
Which line is accepted by the compiler?
hints: Which line checks the value first?
questions.onCorrect: The typeof test narrows input to string inside the branch, which makes the call legal.

choices.label: input.trim();
if (typeof input === "string") input.trim();
input.length;
const n: number = input;

misconceptions.feedback: A value of type unknown has no methods until it is narrowed.
length is not allowed on unknown, because it might not have one.
unknown is not assignable to number without a check or an assertion.

hints: The option makes every index read admit a missing element.
questions.onCorrect: The checker cannot know the length, so with the option on it adds undefined to every index read.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the type when the option is off. With it on, an index read may find nothing.

questions.prompt:
const o = { retries: 3 } satisfies { retries: number | string };
What is the type of o.retries?
hints: satisfies checks the value and does not replace its type.
questions.onCorrect: The inferred type of 3 in a mutable property is number, and satisfies leaves it alone.

misconceptions.feedback: An annotation would give that wider type. satisfies keeps the type the value already had.

questions.prompt:
In Node, a program runs these four expressions: typeof window, typeof document, typeof process, typeof fetch.
How many of them give the string "undefined"?
hints: Which of the four belong to a web page?
process is specific to Node.
Count the ones that Node does not provide.
questions.onCorrect: window and document come from the browser, so Node leaves them undefined, while process and fetch exist.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Node has no window and no document, so those two give "undefined". It has process, and it has fetch, so those two give "object" and "function".

misconceptions.feedback: window and document belong to the browser's page, and Node runs no page.
Both window and document are missing in Node.
process is Node's own global, and fetch is provided as well.
process and fetch both exist in Node.

questions.prompt: In a file that Node runs as an ES module, what is typeof __dirname?
hints: typeof on a name that does not exist is safe.
questions.onCorrect: The ES module system does not provide __dirname, and import.meta.dirname takes its place.

choices.label: 'string'
'undefined'
'function'
a ReferenceError is thrown

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value in a CommonJS module, where Node supplies it.
That is typeof require in CommonJS. __dirname is a string there, not a function.
typeof is safe on a name that was never declared, so nothing is thrown.

questions.prompt: In an ES module, which property of import.meta holds the path of the folder that contains the file? Give the property name.
hints: It replaces the CommonJS name that has underscores.
It is a short word for the directory.
questions.onCorrect: import.meta.dirname is available in ES modules from Node 20.11 and 21.2, and replaces __dirname.

misconceptions.feedback: The name with underscores exists only in CommonJS. The ES module form has none.

hints: Look for the node: prefix.
A bare name is a package and a name with a dot is a file.
Count the node: specifiers.
questions.onCorrect: The node: prefix marks a built-in, so the count is of specifiers that start with it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The specifiers beginning with node: are built-in modules, so node:path and node:http are. express is a package and ./path.js is a file of your own, even though its name contains path.

misconceptions.feedback: Two of the specifiers start with node:.
A name that contains path is not a built-in. Only the node: prefix marks one.
express and ./path.js are not part of Node.

hints: Where do environment variables get their values from?
They are text, as they are in a shell.
questions.onCorrect: process.env stores strings only, so the number 5 becomes the string "5" on assignment.

misconceptions.feedback: Environment variables are text, so the assignment stores the characters 5, and not the number.

hints: Is the variable set?
What does ?? do for undefined?
Convert the result with Number.
questions.onCorrect: ?? replaces an undefined left side with the default, which Number then leaves as it is.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: PORT is undefined, so ?? supplies 3000, and Number(3000) is 3000.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero would be Number of an empty string. Here the variable is missing, not empty.
Nothing here counts anything. The default is supplied by the operator ??.

hints: The variable is set, but to nothing.
?? replaces undefined and null only.
What is Number of an empty string?
questions.onCorrect: A variable that is set to nothing is an empty string, which ?? keeps, so the conversion gives 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The empty string is not undefined, so ?? keeps it, and Number("") is 0. Using || instead would replace the empty string and print 3000.

misconceptions.feedback: ?? replaces only undefined and null. An empty string is neither, so the default is not used.
No value of 8080 appears here. The variable holds the empty string.

questions.prompt: Which kind of file does Node always treat as CommonJS, whatever the package.json says?
hints: One extension is the CommonJS counterpart of .mjs.
questions.onCorrect: The .cjs extension marks CommonJS in the same way that .mjs marks an ES module.

choices.label: .cjs
.mjs
.json
.ts

misconceptions.feedback: A .mjs file is always an ES module.
A .json file is data, and Node reads it as JSON.
Node does not run .ts files by itself in the usual way, so the extension decides nothing here.

hints: Is the value of RETRIES a number?
What does + do when one side is a string?
Join the text 3 with the text 1.
questions.onCorrect: Environment values are strings, so + joins them, which is why they must be converted with Number first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RETRIES is the string "3", and + joins a string and a number, so the result is the string "31".

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the sum of two numbers, but the left side is a string.
Adding 1 changes the result, because + joins the text.

hints: Is there such a variable?
Reading a missing property gives a special value.
questions.onCorrect: A variable that is not set is simply absent from process.env, so reading it gives undefined.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing environment variable is not null. Reading it gives the value JavaScript uses for an absent property.

hints: The code that is running now finishes first.
Two queues run before the loop moves on, one after the other.
Count the lines in the order they run.
questions.onCorrect: The queues run in order after the current code, nextTick first and then promises, and the timer waits for a later phase.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The synchronous line prints first. Then the nextTick queue runs, then the promise queue, and the timer comes later, so the order is sync, tick, promise, timeout, which puts promise third.

misconceptions.feedback: A promise callback waits for the nextTick queue, which runs before it.
Even a zero-delay promise callback waits until the current code has finished.
A promise callback runs before the loop moves to the timers phase.

hints: List the synchronous lines first.
Then the nextTick queue, then the promise queue.
The timer is last, so count the others.
questions.onCorrect: A zero-delay timer waits for the timers phase, which comes after the synchronous code and both queues.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two synchronous lines print first, a then e. Then the nextTick queue gives d, then the promise queue gives c, and the timer is last: a, e, d, c, b.

misconceptions.feedback: The timer waits for a later phase of the loop, after the synchronous code and both queues.
Two queues run before the timer, so more than two lines come before it.
The timer comes after the nextTick and the promise callbacks.

questions.prompt: Inside an fs.readFile callback you call setTimeout(f, 0) and setImmediate(g). Which runs first?
hints: Which phase comes after the poll phase?
questions.onCorrect: The check phase follows the poll phase, so setImmediate runs before the next timers phase.

choices.label: f, the timer
g, the setImmediate callback
Either, it is random
Neither runs

misconceptions.feedback: The loop is in the poll phase, so the timers phase does not come again until after the check phase.
That is the order from the main script. Inside an I/O callback the order is fixed.
Both callbacks are queued, so both run.

questions.prompt: Why does the nextTick callback run before the promise callback in a CommonJS file?
hints: The queues have a fixed order between them.
questions.onCorrect: The two queues are emptied in a fixed order, nextTick first and then promises, whichever was registered first.

choices.label: Node empties the nextTick queue first, and the promise queue after it.
Promises always wait for a timer to fire first.
The tick callback was written first in the file.
nextTick callbacks run on a second thread.

acceptedIdeas: Node empties the nextTick queue first, and the promise queue after it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Node empties the nextTick queue first, and the promise queue after it.

misconceptions.feedback: Promise callbacks do not wait for timers. They run in the queue before the loop moves on.
The order of writing does not decide it. The tick queue would still go first if the promise line came first.
All the JavaScript runs on one thread, including the nextTick callbacks.

questions.prompt: How many callbacks were waiting when the script finished running its synchronous code?
hints: Count the calls that register a callback.
Do not count the line that logs sync directly.
Add the timer, the nextTick callback and the promise callback.
questions.onCorrect: The script registers three callbacks and logs once directly, so three are waiting afterwards.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The nextTick callback, the promise callback and the timer callback were all waiting, which makes three.

misconceptions.feedback: The script registered three callbacks, and each one waited for the synchronous code to finish.
The fourth line, sync, was run directly by the script, so it was not waiting.

questions.prompt:
A timer is set for 10 ms. Then a synchronous loop that runs for 1000 ms starts on the same thread.
At the earliest, after how many milliseconds can the timer callback run?
hints: Only one callback can run at a time.
The loop is running when the timer becomes due.
When does the thread become free?
questions.onCorrect: A due timer waits for the thread, so a blocking loop sets the earliest time the callback can run.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The callback cannot start until the loop has finished and given the thread back, so it runs after 1000 ms at the earliest.

misconceptions.feedback: The timer is due at 10 ms, but a due callback still needs the thread, which the loop is using.
The loop and the timer count down together, so the callback does not wait for both of them in turn.

questions.prompt: Which Node built-in module runs a JavaScript file on a separate thread? Give its name without the node: prefix.
hints: Its name says what it creates.
It uses underscores.
questions.onCorrect: worker_threads gives JavaScript a second thread inside the same process, which suits CPU-bound work.

misconceptions.feedback: That module starts a separate process, not a thread. The module wanted runs another thread of the same process.

hints: The synchronous line goes first.
Which of the two queues is emptied first?
p is in the other one.
questions.onCorrect: In CommonJS the nextTick queue is emptied before the promise queue, which puts p last.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: s prints first, then the nextTick queue gives n, and the promise queue gives p last: s, n, p.

misconceptions.feedback: The synchronous line runs before any queued callback.
In a CommonJS file the nextTick queue runs before the promise queue.

questions.prompt: A request handler hashes a 200 MB file with a long synchronous loop, and other requests stall. What is the best fix?
hints: The problem is that the main thread is busy.
Which fix gives the work another thread?
questions.onCorrect: Only a second thread or process frees the main one, since the work is computation and not waiting.

choices.label: Wrap the loop in async/await.
Move the work to a worker thread or a separate process.
Use setTimeout(0) inside the loop body.
Add more await keywords.

acceptedIdeas: Move the work to a worker thread or a separate process.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Move the work to a worker thread or a separate process.

misconceptions.feedback: async and await do not move the loop to another thread. The loop still holds the only thread.
setTimeout adds delays, but each slice of the loop still runs on the main thread.
await waits for promises, and a CPU-bound loop has none to wait for.

questions.prompt:
A handler runs a synchronous loop that takes 200 ms for each request. Ten requests arrive at the same moment.
At the earliest, after how many milliseconds can the tenth response be sent?
hints: One thread handles one request at a time.
Each takes 200 ms.
Multiply by the number of requests.
questions.onCorrect: With one thread and no waiting to overlap, the times add up, so the tenth response is sent at ten times 200 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The requests are handled one after another on one thread, so ten requests take 10 * 200 = 2000 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for a single request. The tenth waits for the nine before it.
The tenth request's own 200 ms must also be done before its response is sent.

questions.prompt:
const s = "héllo";
Buffer.byteLength(s) counts the bytes the string takes in UTF-8. How many bytes is that?
hints: Most of the letters are plain ASCII.
An accented letter takes more than one byte in UTF-8.
Add the bytes of each character.
questions.onCorrect: UTF-8 spends one byte on each ASCII letter and two on é, so the size is 6 bytes for 5 characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four ASCII letters take one byte each, and the accented é takes two, which makes 6, although the string has 5 characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the string. The accented letter is not one of the one-byte characters.
Each letter does not take two bytes. Only the accented one does.

questions.prompt:
Buffer.byteLength("naïve€")
The string has six characters: n, a, ï, v, e and the euro sign. The ï takes two bytes and the euro sign takes three. How many bytes is the string in UTF-8?
hints: Count the ASCII letters first.
Add two bytes for ï and three for the euro sign.
Add the three amounts together.
questions.onCorrect: The size is the sum over the characters, with one byte for each ASCII letter and more for the others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four ASCII letters take 4 bytes, the ï takes 2 and the euro sign takes 3, so the total is 4 + 2 + 3 = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of characters. Two of them take more than one byte.
The euro sign takes three bytes, one more than that.

questions.prompt:
console.log(Buffer.from("hi").toString("base64"));
What is printed?
hints: The bytes of hi are 68 and 69.
Base64 ends the text with = padding when the bytes are not a multiple of three.
questions.onCorrect: Two bytes fill less than a full group of three, so base64 pads the four characters with an equals sign.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hex form of the same two bytes. The question asks for the other encoding.

questions.prompt:
A file is 1 MiB, which is 1048576 bytes. A read stream delivers it in chunks of 65536 bytes.
How many chunks does the stream deliver?
hints: Divide the file size by the chunk size.
Both sizes are powers of two.
Divide the larger number by the smaller.
questions.onCorrect: The file divides into 16 chunks of 65536 bytes, which is what the stream would deliver.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1048576 divided by 65536 is 16, so the stream delivers 16 chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be readFile, which gives the whole file at once. A stream delivers it in pieces.
That divides by 16384 instead. Check the chunk size in the question.

hints: Add up the bytes waiting after each call.
A call returns false when that total reaches 10 or more.
Count the calls that reach it.
questions.onCorrect: The signal appears as soon as the waiting bytes reach the mark, and it stays while they remain at or above it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the first write 5 bytes are waiting, below the mark, so it returns true. The second brings the total to 10, which reaches the mark, and the third goes over it, so two calls return false.

misconceptions.feedback: A write returns false once the waiting bytes reach the mark, and the second one does.
The third write adds to a buffer that is already at the mark, so it returns false as well.
The first write leaves 5 bytes waiting, which is below the mark.

hints: Add the bytes after each call.
The mark is 10.
Find the first total that reaches it.
questions.onCorrect: The signal depends on the running total, and 12 is the first total that is at least 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After two writes 8 bytes are waiting, below the mark. The third adds 4 more, giving 12, which is over the mark, so it is the first to return false.

misconceptions.feedback: After two writes only 8 bytes are waiting, which is still below the mark of 10.
Four bytes waiting is below the mark.

questions.prompt: Why is pipeline preferred to calling write() in a loop over the chunks?
hints: Which signal must a manual loop remember to check?
questions.onCorrect: pipeline handles the two things a hand-written loop usually forgets: the pause on false, and the cleanup on error.

choices.label: It respects backpressure and cleans up all the streams if one of them fails.
It runs each stage on its own thread.
It reads the whole file first so that the stages need no limits.
It converts every chunk to base64.

acceptedIdeas: It respects backpressure and cleans up all the streams if one of them fails.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It respects backpressure and cleans up all the streams if one of them fails.

misconceptions.feedback: The stages still run on the one JavaScript thread.
Reading the whole file first is what streams exist to avoid.
pipeline does not change the encoding of the data.

questions.prompt: How many streams does the call pipeline(source, transform, destination) connect?
hints: Count the arguments.
Each one is a stream.
Add them up.
questions.onCorrect: The call lists one stream per stage, so three streams are connected.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It connects the three streams that are named: the source, the transform and the destination.

misconceptions.feedback: The transform in the middle is a stream as well, so it is counted.
Three streams are named in the call.

questions.prompt:
A text file contains 1000 characters. 600 of them are the letter é and 400 are plain ASCII letters. It is saved as UTF-8.
How many bytes is the file?
hints: Count the bytes for the accented letters.
Count the bytes for the ASCII letters.
Add the two amounts.
questions.onCorrect: The file's size is the sum of its characters' byte sizes, and it is larger than the number of characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each é takes 2 bytes, so 600 of them take 1200 bytes, and the 400 ASCII letters take 400 more, giving 1600 bytes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one byte for every character, which is true only for ASCII.
Only the accented letters take two bytes. The ASCII ones take one.

questions.prompt:
Buffer.byteLength("ñandú")
The string has five characters, and ñ and ú take two bytes each in UTF-8. How many bytes is it?
hints: Count the plain ASCII letters.
Count the two accented ones twice.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The byte count is higher than the length by one for each two-byte character.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three ASCII letters take 3 bytes, and ñ and ú take 2 each, which gives 3 + 2 + 2 = 7.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the string's length. Two of the characters take two bytes.
Only ñ and ú take two bytes. The other letters take one.

questions.prompt:
console.log(Buffer.from("6869", "hex").toString());
What is printed?
hints: 6869 is the hex form of two bytes.
68 and 69 are the codes of two letters.
questions.onCorrect: Decoding hex gives the bytes 68 and 69, which UTF-8 reads as the letters h and i.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the input. The hex is decoded to bytes, and the bytes are read back as text.

questions.prompt: A producer calls write() on a stream and it returns false. What should the producer do?
hints: False means that the buffer has reached its limit.
questions.onCorrect: False asks the producer to pause, and the drain event says when the buffer has emptied and writing may resume.

choices.label: Stop writing until the stream emits drain.
Keep writing, because false means the data was lost.
Call write() again immediately with the same data.
Close the stream.

acceptedIdeas: Stop writing until the stream emits drain.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stop writing until the stream emits drain.

misconceptions.feedback: The data was accepted. False is a request to slow down, not a report of loss.
Writing the same data again would duplicate it.
Nothing is wrong with the stream. It is full for the moment.

hints: req.url includes the query string.
Find the third piece after splitting on slashes.
Count the characters in that piece.
questions.onCorrect: req.url holds the whole target, query string included, so the last piece is not just the id.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Splitting "/users/42?x=1" on slashes gives "", "users" and "42?x=1", and the last piece has the characters 4, 2, ?, x, =, 1, which is 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the length of 42 alone. req.url still includes the query string.
That is the length of the whole URL. The split takes the third piece only.

hints: The URL class separates the query string from the path.
Split the pathname on slashes.
Take the piece at index 2.
questions.onCorrect: Parsing with URL removes the query string, so the id is a clean piece of the pathname.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pathname is /users/42, without the query string, so splitting on slashes gives "", "users" and "42", and parts[2] is 42.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of the query parameter x. The id is in the path.
The piece at index 2 is the id, which is the number after users.

questions.prompt:
A client sends a POST whose body is not valid JSON, and the handler cannot parse it.
Which status code should the server return?
hints: Whose mistake is it, the client's or the server's?
That class of code starts with 4.
Which 4xx code means a malformed request?
questions.onCorrect: A body that cannot be parsed is a client error, and 400 is the code for a request the server cannot understand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The request itself is malformed, which is the client's mistake, so the right code is 400 Bad Request.

misconceptions.feedback: The fault is in the request, not in the server, so a 4xx code is right.
The path exists. What is wrong is the content of the body.
That would say the request succeeded.

questions.prompt: Why is the DELETE answered with 405 and not 404?
hints: What does Allow say?
questions.onCorrect: 405 tells the client that the resource is there and lists in Allow the methods that it accepts.

choices.label: The path exists, and it is the method that is not allowed there.
The user does not exist.
405 is used for every request that has a body.
The server has failed to start.

acceptedIdeas: The path exists, and it is the method that is not allowed there.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The path exists, and it is the method that is not allowed there.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing user is a 404 on the GET route, which is a different situation.
The status depends on the method and the path, not on the body.
A failure of the server itself would be a 5xx.

questions.prompt: Which status code does the service return for the DELETE request?
hints: The path exists.
The method is not allowed on it.
Which 4xx code is named for that?
questions.onCorrect: 405 is the code for a known path with an unsupported method.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The path exists but the method is not allowed, so the answer is 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow header listing GET.

misconceptions.feedback: The path /users/42 does exist. Only the method is wrong.
The request is well formed. It is the method that the route does not accept.

questions.prompt: A handler calls res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/plain" }) and res.write("ok") but never calls res.end(). What does the client see?

questions.onCorrect: Only res.end() completes a response, so the connection stays open until the client or a proxy gives up.

choices.label: The full response "ok" immediately.
The response never completes, and the client waits until something times out.
A 500 error from Node.
An empty 204 response.

acceptedIdeas: The response never completes, and the client waits until something times out.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The response never completes, and the client waits until something times out.

misconceptions.feedback: Without end, the response is not complete, so the client cannot treat it as finished.
Node raises no error for a response that is left open.
Node does not turn an open response into a 204.

questions.prompt: Which built-in function throws a SyntaxError when it is given text that is not valid JSON? Give the function in the form Object.method.
hints: It reads text and produces a value.
It belongs to the JSON object.
questions.onCorrect: JSON.parse throws on invalid text, and a handler catches the error and answers 400.

questions.prompt:
A handler finds no user for the id and calls res.end("not found") without setting a status.
What status code does the client receive?
hints: What is the default of res.statusCode?
Did the handler change it?
The answer is the default value.
questions.onCorrect: A missing status is not an error to Node, so the response is a success with an unhelpful body.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The default status is 200, and nothing set another, so the client is told that the request succeeded.

misconceptions.feedback: The handler never sets 404. Node's default is a success code.
Node does not choose 500 for a handler that finished normally.

hints: Parse the URL, then use the pathname only.
Split the pathname on slashes.
Take the piece at index 2.
questions.onCorrect: The pathname holds the id and the query string holds the options, so parts[2] is the id.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pathname is /orders/7, so splitting gives "", "orders" and "7", and parts[2] is 7. The page value is in the query string.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the page number, which is in the query string and not in the path.
The query string is separate from the pathname. Parsing with URL keeps it out of the pieces.

questions.prompt:
A client sends a POST to /users with a valid body, and the server creates the user.
Which status code should the server return?
hints: The request succeeded.
Something new was created.
Which 2xx code says so?
questions.onCorrect: 201 is the success code for a creation, and the Location header points to the new resource.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A successful creation is answered with 201 Created, usually with a Location header that names the new resource.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a success, but a more specific code says that something new was made.
204 means there is nothing to send back, and a creation usually returns where the new resource is.

questions.prompt: A handler calls res.setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json") and res.write(JSON.stringify({ ok: true })) and then returns. What should it do differently?
hints: What marks a response as finished?
questions.onCorrect: The response is complete only when res.end() has been called, and a handler that returns without it leaves the client waiting.

choices.label: Call res.end() so that the response is completed.
Return a number so that Node sends it.
Set the status to 500 so that Node finishes.
Call res.write a second time.

acceptedIdeas: Call res.end() so that the response is completed.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Call res.end() so that the response is completed.

misconceptions.feedback: The return value of a handler is ignored by Node.
A different status does not complete a response.
Writing more does not complete a response either.

hints: One of the three promises rejects.
What does Promise.all do when one input rejects?
questions.onCorrect: Promise.all rejects with the error of the first promise to reject, without waiting for the others.

misconceptions.feedback: The array of values is produced only when every promise fulfils. One of them rejects, so the call throws instead.

hints: allSettled reports one entry per task.
Each entry carries its own task's outcome.
Count the tasks that rejected.
questions.onCorrect: Every outcome is kept, so the rejections show up as entries with the status rejected.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: allSettled gives one entry for each of the four tasks, and the entries for b and d have the status rejected, so two do.

misconceptions.feedback: allSettled does not turn every outcome into a rejection. Each entry reports its own task's outcome.
allSettled itself does not reject, but the entries for the rejected tasks say so.
Both b and d rejected, and each has its own entry.

questions.prompt:
Three independent tasks each take 50 ms. They are awaited one after another in a for loop.
Ignoring overhead, how many milliseconds until all three have finished?
hints: Does the second task start before the first ends?
In a loop, each await finishes before the next task begins.
Add the three durations.
questions.onCorrect: Sequential awaits add up, so the total is the sum of the durations.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each task starts when the one before it has finished, so the times add: 50 + 50 + 50 = 150 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for one task. In a loop the next one starts only after the previous one.
All three tasks have to finish, so there are three delays to add.

hints: The callback pauses at await.
Does forEach wait for the promise it returns?
What is in the list when the log runs?
questions.onCorrect: The pushes happen after the log, because the log runs in the same turn as the forEach call.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: forEach does not wait for the promises its callback returns, so the log runs before any of the callbacks has resumed after its await, and the list is still empty.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be so if the pushes had finished. forEach did not wait for them.
None of the callbacks has resumed after its await when the log runs.

questions.prompt: Why does forEach not wait for an async callback?
hints: What does forEach do with a return value?
questions.onCorrect: forEach throws away what its callback returns, and so the promise is lost and nothing waits for it.

choices.label: It does not use the value the callback returns, so the promise is dropped.
Callbacks given to forEach always run in the background.
await is not allowed inside a forEach callback.
forEach waits only for the first callback.

acceptedIdeas: It does not use the value the callback returns, so the promise is dropped.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It does not use the value the callback returns, so the promise is dropped.

misconceptions.feedback: The callbacks run in the same thread, one at a time, and are not moved to the background.
await is allowed in an async callback. The issue is who waits for the callback.
forEach calls every callback and waits for none of them.

questions.prompt: What does out.length print after the fix, once Promise.all has finished?
hints: The fix waits for every promise.
Each callback pushes once.
Count the pushes.
questions.onCorrect: Collecting the promises with map and waiting with Promise.all makes every push happen before the next line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three callbacks have completed their push before the log, so the list holds 1, 2 and 3, which is three items.

misconceptions.feedback: Promise.all waits for all the callbacks, so the pushes are done before the log.
Every callback pushes once, and all three were waited for.

questions.prompt:
node -e "Promise.reject(new Error('x'))"
No handler is registered anywhere. What exit code does the process end with?
hints: Is the rejection handled anywhere?
What is the default action for one that is not?
A failure has a non-zero code, and Node uses the lowest.
questions.onCorrect: The default action turns the rejection into an uncaught exception, which exits with code 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection ends the process with a non-zero code, and the code is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: Exit code 0 would mean success. Node treats the rejection as an uncaught error.
Node uses a lower code than that for an uncaught error.

hints: The error is named after the action.
It ends with Error.
questions.onCorrect: An aborted operation rejects with an error named AbortError, which code can check by name.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are errors of other kinds. An operation stopped by a signal rejects with an error named for the abort.

questions.prompt:
Three independent tasks take 30 ms, 50 ms and 20 ms. They are started together and awaited with Promise.all.
Ignoring overhead, how many milliseconds until all three have finished?
hints: The tasks overlap.
Promise.all waits for the slowest of them.
Find the largest duration.
questions.onCorrect: Overlapping waits finish with the longest task, and the total is the maximum, not the sum.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They overlap, so the call finishes when the slowest task does, which is 50 ms. Awaited one after another they would take 100 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total for awaiting them one after another. Started together, they overlap.
The call waits for every task, so it ends with the slowest, not the first.

hints: Each entry reports its own promise.
The promise in the list rejects.
questions.onCorrect: allSettled keeps the outcome of each promise, with the status string rejected for the one that failed.

misconceptions.feedback: allSettled itself fulfils, but each entry reports the outcome of its own promise.

hints: Does the loop wait at each await?
Each pass pushes one number.
Count the passes.
questions.onCorrect: The loop itself pauses and resumes, which forEach does not, so the list is full.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A for loop with await pauses at each await and continues afterwards, so all three pushes have happened before the log.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result with forEach. A for loop does wait at each await.
The loop goes on through all three elements before the log runs.

questions.prompt:
Two versions of a library exist, 1.9.0 and 1.10.0.
Enter the minor number of the newer one.
hints: Version parts are numbers, not text.
Compare the two minor parts as numbers.
Take the larger.
questions.onCorrect: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0 because the minor parts are compared as whole numbers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Version parts are compared as numbers, so 10 is greater than 9, and 1.10.0 is the newer version. Its minor number is 10.

misconceptions.feedback: Compared as text, "9" sorts after "1", but version parts are compared as numbers, and the larger number wins.

questions.prompt: What is the next minor version after 1.4.2? Give it as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
hints: Raise the middle number by one.
Raising a part resets the parts to its right.
questions.onCorrect: A minor bump raises the middle number and resets the patch number to 0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the next patch version. A minor bump raises the middle number.

questions.prompt:
The range is ^1.2.3. Five versions are offered: 1.2.2, 1.2.9, 1.9.0, 2.0.0 and 1.2.3-beta.1.
How many of them does the range accept?
hints: ^1.2.3 means at least 1.2.3 and below 2.0.0.
Prereleases are excluded unless named.
Check each version against both ends.
questions.onCorrect: The range has a lower end at 1.2.3 and an upper end at the next major, and prereleases are left out.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The range accepts 1.2.9 and 1.9.0. It rejects 1.2.2, which is older than 1.2.3, 2.0.0, which is the next major, and the prerelease 1.2.3-beta.1.

misconceptions.feedback: The prerelease 1.2.3-beta.1 is older than 1.2.3 and is not offered to a range that does not name one.
The older 1.2.2 and the next major 2.0.0 fall outside the range.
Both 1.2.9 and 1.9.0 are above 1.2.3 and below the next major version.

questions.prompt: Why does the caret fix the minor part for ^0.2.3, when it fixed the major part for ^1.2.3?
hints: What does semver say about versions before 1.0.0?
questions.onCorrect: Before 1.0.0 the library may change freely, so the caret treats the first non-zero part as the one that marks a breaking change.

choices.label: Below 1.0.0 the library is not yet stable, so a minor change may break callers.
Because the version 0.2.3 has no major part.
Because the caret always fixes the middle number.
Because npm cannot install a major version of 0.

acceptedIdeas: Below 1.0.0 the library is not yet stable, so a minor change may break callers.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Below 1.0.0 the library is not yet stable, so a minor change may break callers.

misconceptions.feedback: The major part exists and is 0. The rule is about which part is the first non-zero one.
For ^1.2.3 the middle number is allowed to rise.
npm installs versions below 1.0.0 without trouble.

questions.prompt: How many of the four candidates, 0.2.2, 0.2.3, 0.2.9 and 0.3.0, does ^0.2.3 accept?
hints: The range is at least 0.2.3 and below 0.3.0.
Check each candidate against it.
Count the ones that fit.
questions.onCorrect: The accepted candidates are the lower end and the one between the ends.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 0.2.3 and 0.2.9 lie between the lower end 0.2.3 and the upper end 0.3.0, which is excluded.

misconceptions.feedback: The lower end 0.2.3 is accepted, and so is 0.2.9.
The upper end is excluded, and 0.2.2 is below the lower end.

questions.prompt: Which npm command installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json, and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree? Give the command.
hints: It is the command a build server uses.
Its name is two letters long.
questions.onCorrect: npm ci installs the lockfile exactly and fails on a mismatch, which gives repeatable builds.

misconceptions.feedback: npm install may pick newer versions that a range allows and rewrite the lockfile. The command wanted does neither.

hints: A test fails when its assertion throws.
strictEqual uses ===.
Check each assertion on its own.
questions.onCorrect: Each failing assertion makes its own test fail, and strictEqual does not convert types.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Test b fails because 4 is not 5. Test d fails because strictEqual uses ===, and the string "5" is not the number 5. Tests a and c pass.

misconceptions.feedback: Check test d: strictEqual compares with ===, and a string is not equal to a number.
Two of the assertions compare values that are not strictly equal.
Test a adds correctly and test c compares objects with equal contents, so both pass.

questions.prompt:
A library fixes a crash and changes nothing else that callers see. Its current version is 3.2.1.
What version should it release? Give MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
hints: A bug fix is the smallest kind of change.
Which of the three parts is raised for it?
questions.onCorrect: A fix that changes no behaviour callers depend on raises only the patch number.

misconceptions.feedback: Those would announce a new feature or a breaking change. A bug fix alone raises the last number.

questions.prompt: Which version does the range ^1.2.3 accept?
hints: The range runs from 1.2.3 up to the next major version.
questions.onCorrect: The caret allows any version from 1.2.3 up to, but not including, 2.0.0, so 1.9.0 is inside.

misconceptions.feedback: 2.0.0 is the next major version, which the caret excludes.
1.2.2 is older than the lower end of the range.
A prerelease is not accepted unless the range names one.

questions.prompt:
The range is ~2.4.1. Four versions are offered: 2.4.0, 2.4.9, 2.5.0 and 3.0.0.
How many of them does the range accept?
hints: ~2.4.1 means at least 2.4.1 and below 2.5.0.
Check each version against both ends.
Count those that fit.
questions.onCorrect: A tilde range stays within the minor version it names, and starts at the stated patch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A tilde range accepts patch changes only, from 2.4.1 up to but not including 2.5.0, so only 2.4.9 is accepted. 2.4.0 is below the lower end.

misconceptions.feedback: 2.4.0 is older than 2.4.1, so it is outside the range.
2.5.0 is a minor change, which the tilde does not allow.
2.4.9 lies between the lower end and 2.5.0.

questions.prompt: What is the next major version after 1.4.2? Give it as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
hints: Raise the first number by one.
The two numbers to its right go back to zero.
questions.onCorrect: A major bump raises the first number and resets the minor and patch numbers to 0.

misconceptions.feedback: Those raise the minor or the patch part. A major bump raises the first number and resets the other two.

hints: Check PORT first, then DATABASE_URL.
Number("abc") is not an integer.
Count the problems added.
questions.onCorrect: Each check runs, so every problem is collected, and one error reports them all.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Number("abc") is NaN, which is not an integer, so the first problem is added, and DATABASE_URL is missing, so the second is added too. The error lists both.

misconceptions.feedback: The checks do not stop at the first problem. Look at both conditions.
An empty list would not throw. Check each condition against the input.

questions.prompt:
console.log(Number("80x"));
What is printed?
hints: Number must convert the whole string.
Some strings are not numbers at all.
questions.onCorrect: Number gives NaN for text that is not a whole number, and Number.isInteger(NaN) is false, so the check catches it.

misconceptions.feedback: Number converts the whole string, and a string that is not a complete number gives the special value, not the part that parses.

questions.prompt: What does the cast in JSON.parse(text) as CreateUser check about the value at run time? Answer in one word.
hints: Is the cast still there when the program runs?
It adds no code.
questions.onCorrect: An assertion changes only what the checker believes, so it tests nothing when the program runs.

misconceptions.feedback: A cast is erased when the code is compiled, so it adds no test of any kind.

hints: Both fields must be present and of the right type.
Zero is a number.
Check each body against both rules.
questions.onCorrect: A parser accepts only when every field passes, and a falsy value such as 0 is still a valid number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Bodies 1 and 4 have a string name and a number age. Body 2 has no age, and body 3 has a number where the name should be a string, so both fail.

misconceptions.feedback: Body 4 has an age of zero, which is still a number, so it passes.
One of the bodies has no age, and another has a name that is not a string.
Two of the bodies break the rules of the parser.

questions.prompt:
A request takes 300 ms to answer. 50 ms after it starts, the process gets SIGTERM, and its handler calls server.close() and does not call process.exit().
How many milliseconds after the request started is its response delivered?
hints: server.close() refuses new connections only.
A request in flight is allowed to finish.
When would it have finished without the signal?
questions.onCorrect: Graceful shutdown stops new work and lets current work end, so the in-flight request keeps its original time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: server.close() stops new connections but lets requests that are already running finish, so the response is delivered at 300 ms as planned.

misconceptions.feedback: The request is not cut off when SIGTERM arrives. close() lets work in flight finish.
The signal does not add to the time. The request carries on and finishes as planned.

questions.prompt:
A graceful shutdown has four steps: A stop accepting new connections, B wait for requests in flight, C close the database pool, D exit with code 0.
In the correct order, in which position does C come?
hints: New work must stop first.
A resource is closed after everything that uses it has finished.
Exit comes last.
questions.onCorrect: The pool is closed only after the requests that use it have finished, and before the process exits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A comes first so that no new work arrives, B waits for current work, C closes the pool once nothing uses it, and D exits, which puts C third.

misconceptions.feedback: Closing the pool first would break the requests that are still using it.
The pool is still in use while requests are in flight, so it cannot be closed before B.
Exiting ends the process, so the pool must be closed before it.

questions.prompt: Why does the test file include bad input as well as good?
hints: What is the parser for?
questions.onCorrect: A parser is useful only if it refuses what it should and accepts what it should, so both cases are tested.

choices.label: The boundary exists to refuse bad input, so a test of it must send some.
Bad input makes the tests run faster.
node:test requires at least one failing test.
Good input does not need to be tested.

acceptedIdeas: The boundary exists to refuse bad input, so a test of it must send some.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The boundary exists to refuse bad input, so a test of it must send some.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed does not depend on the data in this way.
A failing test is a fault, and the runner reports it as one.
The success case matters too, because a parser that refuses everything would pass the failure tests.

questions.prompt: How many different failure messages can parseCreateUser give?
hints: Count the checks in the parser.
Each one has a message.
Add them up.
questions.onCorrect: One test per message, plus the success case, covers every path through the parser.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It can report that the body is not an object, that the name is not a string, or that the age is not a number, which makes three.

misconceptions.feedback: Each check has its own message, so there is more than one.
The age check has a message of its own as well.

questions.prompt: Which signal does a platform usually send to ask a service to stop, so that it can shut down gracefully? Give its name.
hints: It is the polite request and not the forced stop.
Its name begins with SIG.
questions.onCorrect: SIGTERM can be handled, which is what makes a graceful shutdown possible, and SIGKILL cannot.

misconceptions.feedback: SIGKILL cannot be caught, so a service has no chance to finish. The signal that asks politely is a different one.

questions.prompt: Where should request-body validation happen so that every handler receives typed data?
hints: Which place sees every request before any handler?
questions.onCorrect: A parser at the boundary runs once for every request, so all handlers receive data that has been checked.

choices.label: Inside each handler after its first query
At the boundary, once, before the handler runs
Only in the database constraints
Nowhere; TypeScript types are enough

acceptedIdeas: At the boundary, once, before the handler runs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the boundary, once, before the handler runs

misconceptions.feedback: By then the unvalidated data has already reached the database.
Constraints are a last defence. They do not give the handler typed data.
Types are erased and cannot check what arrives at run time.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for a graceful SIGTERM shutdown?
hints: Stop the intake of new work first.
Exit comes last.
questions.onCorrect: The intake stops, current work drains, resources are released, and only then does the process exit.

choices.label: Close the database pool, stop accepting connections, wait for requests, exit 0
Stop accepting connections, wait for in-flight requests, close the database pool, exit 0
Exit 0, then close the database pool
Wait for in-flight requests, exit 0, stop accepting connections

acceptedIdeas: Stop accepting connections, wait for in-flight requests, close the database pool, exit 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stop accepting connections, wait for in-flight requests, close the database pool, exit 0

misconceptions.feedback: Closing the pool first breaks the requests that still use it.
Exiting ends the process, so nothing after it runs.
Waiting before stopping the intake lets new requests keep arriving.

questions.prompt:
type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };
How many members does the union Result<number> have?
hints: Count the object types joined by the bar.
One member is for success, the other for failure.
Add them up.
questions.onCorrect: A Result has one member for each outcome, and the ok property tells the checker which one it holds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It has two members, the success member with ok true and a value, and the failure member with ok false and an error.

misconceptions.feedback: A union of success and failure has a member for each.
The two properties value and error belong to the two members, and each member has one.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the removal of annotations, interfaces and aliases when TypeScript is compiled?
flashcards.back: Type erasure: they exist only for the checker, so none of them reach the JavaScript.

flashcards.front: By default, what does tsc do with a file that has a type error?
flashcards.back: It reports the error and still writes the JavaScript, because checking and emitting are separate stages; noEmitOnError changes that.

flashcards.front: Why can instanceof never test an interface?
flashcards.back: The interface is erased, so at run time there is no value for instanceof to use.

flashcards.front: What is the type of const b = 5?
flashcards.back: The literal type 5, because a const never changes and the compiler keeps the exact value.

flashcards.front: Name the type of let a = 5.
flashcards.back: number, because a let can be reassigned and a type of 5 would reject every other number.

flashcards.front: Why is the property kind in const d = { kind: "circle" } typed string?
flashcards.back: The properties of a const object can still change, so the literal widens unless as const freezes the object.

flashcards.front: A class never says it implements an interface. When does its instance fit that interface?
flashcards.back: When it has at least the interface's properties with compatible types, because TypeScript compares shapes.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the check that rejects an unknown property in a fresh object literal?
flashcards.back: The excess property check, a guard against typos that applies only to literals written at the point of use.

flashcards.front: Does readonly stop an assignment when the compiled JavaScript runs?
flashcards.back: No: the modifier is erased, so only the checker enforces it.

flashcards.front: What is a property such as kind, shared by every member of a union and holding a different literal in each, called?
flashcards.back: A discriminant, and a union with one is a discriminated union.

flashcards.front: What type does a value have after every member of its union has been handled?
flashcards.back: never, the type with no values, which is why assigning it to never checks a switch is complete.

flashcards.front: Why does a check like typeof x === "string" narrow x, while x as string does not?
flashcards.back: The check is real code that runs, so the checker can trust it, and an assertion only tells the checker what to believe.

flashcards.front: What does T do in function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined?
flashcards.back: It names a type that each call fills in, so the result type follows from the input type.

flashcards.front: How many arguments to longest<T extends { length: number }> may disagree about T?
flashcards.back: None: both parameters share one T, so the arguments must be compatible with a single type.

flashcards.front: What type does await give for a Promise<number>?
flashcards.back: number: await unwraps the Promise and leaves the type it carries.

flashcards.front: What does keyof T give?
flashcards.back: The union of T's property names as string literals.

flashcards.front: Which utility type removes named properties from an object type?
flashcards.back: Omit<T, K>. Note that it does not check that K names real properties.

flashcards.front: What is the type of typeof Color[keyof typeof Color] for a frozen object of colors?
flashcards.back: The union of the object's values as literal types, which keeps the type and the data in step.

flashcards.front: Why is unknown safer than any for data from outside?
flashcards.back: It accepts every value but allows no use until a check narrows it, while any switches checking off.

flashcards.front: Does value as T convert the value to a T?
flashcards.back: No: it only changes what the checker believes, and adds no code at run time.

flashcards.front: Which compiler option adds undefined to every index read such as xs[0]?
flashcards.back: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, which is not part of strict and has to be turned on by name.

flashcards.front: What does Node add to the JavaScript engine?
flashcards.back: An event loop, file and network APIs, process access and a module system, which together let JavaScript run outside a browser.

flashcards.front: What type is every value in process.env?
flashcards.back: A string, or undefined when the variable is not set.

flashcards.front: Which property replaces __dirname in an ES module?
flashcards.back: import.meta.dirname, since an ES module is not given the CommonJS names.

flashcards.front: Why is async JavaScript in Node not the same as parallel JavaScript?
flashcards.back: All the JavaScript runs on one thread, one callback at a time, and only the waiting for I/O happens elsewhere.

flashcards.front: In a CommonJS file, which runs first after the main script: the nextTick queue or the promise queue?
flashcards.back: The nextTick queue, and then the promise queue, both before the loop moves on.

flashcards.front: Where does CPU-heavy work belong in a Node server?
flashcards.back: In a worker thread or a separate process, so the main thread stays free for callbacks.

flashcards.front: How many bytes does 'héllo' take in UTF-8, and why does it differ from its length?
flashcards.back: Six bytes: the accented é takes two, while length counts UTF-16 code units, which gives 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six bytes: the accented é takes two, while length counts UTF-16 code units, which gives 5.

flashcards.front: What does a false return from write() mean?
flashcards.back: The stream's buffer has reached the high-water mark, so the producer should wait for drain before writing more.

flashcards.front: What is the base64 of the bytes of hi?
flashcards.back: aGk=: two bytes fill less than a group of three, so the output is padded with an equals sign.

flashcards.front: Why should a handler parse req.url with the URL class before routing?
flashcards.back: req.url includes the query string, so '/users/42?x=1' is not equal to '/users/42' until the pathname is taken out.

flashcards.front: Which status code means that a request created something?
flashcards.back: 201 Created, usually with a Location header that names the new resource.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 201 Created, usually with a Location header that names the new resource.

flashcards.front: What happens if a handler returns without calling res.end()?
flashcards.back: The response is never completed, and the client waits until it or a proxy times out.

flashcards.front: What does Promise.all do when one of its promises rejects?
flashcards.back: It rejects at once with that error, and the other tasks keep running but their results are lost.

flashcards.front: Which combinator reports the outcome of every promise, whether it fulfilled or rejected?
flashcards.back: Promise.allSettled, which never rejects and gives a status for each.

flashcards.front: What exit code does Node give when a rejection is never handled?
flashcards.back: 1, because since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is treated as an uncaught error.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1, because since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is treated as an uncaught error.

flashcards.front: Which is newer, 1.10.0 or 1.9.0, and why?
flashcards.back: 1.10.0, because the parts are compared as numbers, and 10 is greater than 9.

flashcards.front: What does ^1.2.3 accept?
flashcards.back: Any version from 1.2.3 up to, but not including, 2.0.0, with prereleases left out.

flashcards.front: Which command installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json?
flashcards.back: npm ci, which also fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree.

flashcards.front: Why does a service read its configuration once, at startup?
flashcards.back: A mistake then stops the service before it has served anything, with every problem listed, instead of failing on a later request.

flashcards.front: How many run-time checks does the cast value as CreateUser add?
flashcards.back: None: the assertion is erased, so only a parser that tests the fields can make the type true.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None: the assertion is erased, so only a parser that tests the fields can make the type true.

flashcards.front: In what order does a graceful shutdown run?
flashcards.back: Stop accepting connections, wait for requests in flight, close resources such as the database pool, then exit with code 0.
